topics.ch: Part I: Nature and Significance of Management
topics.t: Management: getting things done effectively and efficiently
topics.h: A Mumbai dabbawala team delivers lakhs of lunch boxes on time, at very low cost, using simple coding. That is management at work: right result, least waste.
p: Management is the process of getting things done, with the aim of achieving goals effectively and efficiently, through and with other people.
It is a process: a series of linked functions (planning, organising, staffing, directing, controlling).
Effectiveness means doing the right task and completing it on time, that is, achieving the goal.
Efficiency means doing the task correctly with minimum cost, that is, the best use of resources (input vs output).
Both matter: a manager should aim for high effectiveness AND high efficiency. Finishing on time at a huge cost, or saving cost but missing the deadline, is poor management.

ex.q: A firm must make 10,000 school bags by 30 June. It finishes on 25 June, but wastage of cloth pushes cost 20% above budget. Is the firm effective, efficient, both or neither?
st: Effectiveness asks: was the goal achieved on time? Yes, the bags were ready before 30 June.
Efficiency asks: were resources used at minimum cost? No, cost overshot because of wastage.
So the firm was effective but not efficient.

topics.rl: ISRO is admired for both: its Mars Orbiter Mission reached Mars on its first attempt (effective) at a famously low budget (efficient).

rv.summary: Management is the process of getting things done through and with other people to achieve goals effectively and efficiently. A good manager aims for both at the same time.
focus: Define management and explain why it is a process
Tell effectiveness (goal achieved on time) apart from efficiency (minimum cost, best use of resources)
Judge case situations as effective only, efficient only, both or neither
remember: Management: the process of getting things done, with the aim of achieving goals effectively and efficiently, through and with other people
Effectiveness = doing the right task and completing it on time
Efficiency = doing the task correctly with minimum cost (input vs output)
traps: Don't confuse efficiency with effectiveness: meeting a deadline does not prove efficiency
Don't assume a cost saving means the goal was achieved
Management is not just supervision or personal hard work

topics.ch: Part I: Nature and Significance of Management
topics.h: A temple trust, a hospital, a startup and a gram panchayat all look different, yet each needs management. What makes management the same everywhere?
p: Goal-oriented process: every management activity is aimed at achieving set goals.
All-pervasive: needed in all organisations (business, school, hospital, government), at all levels and in all countries.
Multidimensional: it covers management of work, management of people (as individuals and groups) and management of operations.
Continuous: functions are performed again and again; it never stops. Group activity: it works through people with different needs towards common goals.
Dynamic function: it adapts to the changing environment. Intangible force: it cannot be seen, but its presence is felt in order, results and employee satisfaction.

ex.q: A visitor to Sharma Electronics notices that targets are met, staff are cheerful and work flows smoothly, though nobody can 'point to' management. Which characteristic is shown?
st: The visitor cannot see management directly.
Its effect is felt through results and a smooth work environment.
This is the intangible nature of management.

topics.rl: When a smartphone brand in India shifted to selling online during the 2020 lockdown, it showed management as a dynamic function that adapts to change.

rv.summary: Management is a goal-oriented, all-pervasive, multidimensional, continuous, group, dynamic and intangible activity. Each feature can be spotted from a short case.
focus: List and explain all seven characteristics of management
Name the three dimensions: work, people and operations
Identify the characteristic shown in a case
remember: All-pervasive: needed in all organisations, at all levels and in all countries
Multidimensional: management of work, people (individuals and groups) and operations
Dynamic: adapts to the changing environment; intangible: cannot be seen but its presence is felt
traps: Don't confuse all-pervasive (needed everywhere) with dynamic (adapts to change)
Don't add competitors or other outside parties to the dimensions of management
Work and operations are not the same dimension

topics.ch: Part I: Nature and Significance of Management
topics.h: A company can earn crores and still fail if it pollutes the river next door or treats its staff badly. Good management juggles three sets of goals.
p: Organisational objectives: survival (earn enough to cover costs), profit (cover costs and risks, reward owners) and growth (sales, employees, products, capital).
Social objectives: creating benefit for society, e.g. using environment-friendly methods, giving employment to disadvantaged sections, providing basic amenities like schools and creches.
Personal objectives: satisfying employees' needs: financial (competitive salary), social (recognition by peers) and higher-level needs (personal growth and development).
Importance: achieving group goals, increasing efficiency, creating a dynamic organisation (helps people adapt to change), achieving personal objectives, and helping in the development of society.

ex.q: Green Leaf Paper Mill installs a water-recycling plant and runs a free school for workers' children. Which objective is it pursuing?
st: The actions do not directly raise profit or employee pay.
They benefit the environment and the community.
So they fall under social objectives.

topics.rl: Many Indian companies run schools, health camps and water projects near their plants under CSR, a clear example of the social objective of management.

rv.summary: Management has organisational, social and personal objectives. It is important because it helps achieve group goals, raises efficiency, creates a dynamic organisation, meets personal objectives and develops society.
focus: Classify an objective as organisational, social or personal
Explain survival, profit and growth
Explain the five points of importance of management
remember: Organisational objectives: survival, profit and growth
Social objectives: creating benefit for society
Personal objectives: financial, social and higher-level needs of employees
traps: Don't confuse survival (covering costs) with profit (also covering risks and rewarding owners)
Don't assume all employee needs are financial
Don't mix up 'creating a dynamic organisation' with 'increasing efficiency'

topics.ch: Part I: Nature and Significance of Management
topics.t: Management as an art, a science and a profession
topics.h: Two managers read the same textbook, yet one turns a struggling shop around and the other doesn't. Is management a science, an art, or both?
p: Art (features met): existence of theoretical knowledge, personalised application (each manager applies it in her own style) and based on practice and creativity.

Science: a systematised body of knowledge, principles based on experimentation and observation, and universal validity. Management has the first two, but its principles are not exactly universal because it deals with people, so it is an inexact (soft or behavioural) science.
Profession features: well-defined body of knowledge, restricted entry (by an exam or degree), professional association, ethical code of conduct and service motive.

Management meets only some: it has a well-defined body of knowledge, but there is no restricted entry (no degree is legally required to become a manager), membership of associations like AIMA is not compulsory, and its code of conduct is not binding.
Conclusion: management has the features of an art, of an (inexact) science and some features of a profession.

ex.q: Why can't management be called a full profession like law or chartered accountancy?
st: A lawyer must be enrolled with the Bar Council and a CA must be a member of ICAI: entry is restricted.
Anyone can be appointed a manager; an MBA is desirable but not legally required.
Membership of a managers' association is voluntary and its code of conduct is not binding.
So management fails the tests of restricted entry, compulsory professional association and a binding ethical code.
ex.a: It lacks restricted entry, a compulsory professional body and a binding code of conduct

topics.rl: An Indian cricket captain uses the same tactics theory as everyone, but places fielders in a personal style. Like management, captaincy is both a science and an art.

rv.summary: Management has all the features of an art, is an inexact (soft) science because it deals with people, and has only some features of a profession.
focus: Test management against the features of art, science and profession
Explain why management is an inexact science
Explain why management is not a full profession
remember: Art: theoretical knowledge, personalised application, based on practice and creativity
Science: systematised knowledge, principles based on experimentation and observation, universal validity
Profession: body of knowledge, restricted entry, professional association, ethical code, service motive
traps: Don't think management has no principles: they exist but are not exactly universal
AIMA exists, but membership is not compulsory
One profession feature (body of knowledge) is not enough to make management a profession

topics.ch: Part I: Nature and Significance of Management
topics.h: In a large company, who decides to enter a new country, who sets the sales team's monthly duties, and who makes sure the machine operators wear helmets? Three different levels!
p: Levels show the hierarchy of superior-subordinate (authority-responsibility) relationships: top, middle and supervisory (operational).

Top management (chairman, CEO, MD, chief operating officer, president, vice-presidents, board): integrates diverse elements, sets overall goals, strategies and policies, and is responsible for the welfare and survival of the organisation. It analyses the business environment.

Middle management (division or department heads, plant superintendents, operations managers): interprets the policies framed by top management, ensures the department has the necessary personnel, assigns duties, motivates staff and cooperates with other departments. It is the link between top and supervisory levels.

Supervisory or operational management (foremen, supervisors): directly oversees workers, ensures quality of output, minimises wastage, maintains safety standards and passes on workers' problems to higher levels. It links management with the workforce.

ex.q: Identify the level: (i) deciding to set up a plant in Odisha; (ii) assigning sales targets to each regional team; (iii) checking that workers on the shop floor follow safety rules.
st: (i) is a long-term strategic decision, so top management.
(ii) interprets policy and assigns duties, so middle management.
(iii) directly oversees workers, so supervisory management.

topics.rl: In a large Indian bank, the board and managing director set strategy (top), zonal and regional heads turn it into targets for branches (middle), and branch-level officers supervise daily counter work (supervisory).

rv.summary: Management has three levels: top, middle and supervisory (operational). Top sets overall goals and policies, middle interprets them for departments, and supervisors directly oversee workers.
focus: Name the posts at each level
State the functions of each level
Identify the level from a given task
remember: Top management sets overall goals, strategies and policies and is responsible for the organisation's welfare and survival
Middle management interprets policies and links top and supervisory levels
Supervisory management directly oversees workers and links management with the workforce
traps: Don't confuse framing policies (top) with interpreting them (middle)
Don't think department heads supervise workers directly
Don't mix up the links: middle links top and supervisory; supervisory links management and workers

topics.ch: Part I: Nature and Significance of Management
topics.h: Organising a school annual day? You decide what to do, form teams, pick people, guide them, and check if all is on track. You just did all five management functions!
p: Planning: deciding in advance what to do and how to do it. It bridges where we are and where we want to be.
Organising: assigning tasks, grouping them into departments, allocating resources and setting authority relationships.
Staffing: finding and keeping the right people in the right jobs (recruitment, selection, training).
Directing: leading, influencing, motivating and communicating with employees to perform tasks.
Controlling: monitoring performance, comparing it with standards and taking corrective action. The usual sequence is planning, organising, staffing, directing, controlling.

ex.q: A shop owner (i) decides to open a second branch by Diwali, (ii) divides work among three teams, (iii) hires two cashiers, (iv) motivates staff with a festive bonus, (v) checks weekly sales against targets. Name each function.
st: (i) Deciding in advance = planning
(ii) Dividing work = organising
(iii) Hiring = staffing
(iv) Motivating = directing
(v) Comparing with targets = controlling

topics.rl: Before a big IPL season, a franchise plans its strategy, organises support staff, picks players at the auction (staffing), the captain leads them (directing) and analysts track performance (controlling).

rv.summary: The functions of management are planning, organising, staffing, directing and controlling, usually in that order. Planning comes first because the other functions depend on plans.
focus: Define each of the five functions
Identify the function from a given activity
Remember the usual sequence of functions
remember: Sequence: planning, organising, staffing, directing, controlling
Planning: deciding in advance what to do and how to do it
Controlling: monitoring performance, comparing it with standards and taking corrective action
traps: Don't put staffing before organising
Training is part of staffing, not directing
Checking results is controlling, not planning

topics.ch: Part I: Nature and Significance of Management
topics.h: An orchestra has brilliant musicians, but without the conductor it is noise. In business, that conductor is coordination.
p: Coordination is the process by which a manager synchronises the activities of different departments so that group efforts move towards common goals. It is the force that binds all the other functions.

Characteristics: integrates group efforts, ensures unity of action, is a continuous process, is all-pervasive, is the responsibility of all managers and is a deliberate function (it does not happen on its own).

Importance: growth in size (more people and units to link), functional differentiation (departments may pull in different directions) and specialisation (specialists often think only of their own area).
Coordination is called the essence of management because it is needed at all levels (top, middle, supervisory) and in all functions (planning to controlling). It is not a separate function.

ex.q: At Zenith Appliances, production made 50,000 fans but marketing had orders for only 30,000. Which management element was missing, and why does it matter?
st: Each department worked hard but pursued its own target.
There was no matching of production with sales.
Coordination would have synchronised the two departments towards a common goal, avoiding unsold stock.
ex.a: Coordination; it integrates departmental efforts towards common goals

topics.rl: At the Kumbh Mela, railways, police, health services and local bodies must work in step. That synchronisation of many departments is coordination on a giant scale.

rv.summary: Coordination synchronises the activities of different departments so that group efforts move towards common goals. It is the essence of management because it is needed at all levels and in all functions.
focus: Define coordination and list its characteristics
Explain its importance: growth in size, functional differentiation, specialisation
Explain why coordination is called the essence of management
remember: Coordination is the force that binds all the other functions
Coordination is a deliberate function and the responsibility of all managers
Coordination is not a separate function
traps: Don't treat coordination as a separate function or a single step at the end
Cooperation alone is not coordination: it needs conscious effort
Coordination is not only a top management task; it is needed at all levels

topics.t: Principles of management: meaning and nature
topics.h: Traffic rules tell you exactly what to do. Management principles are different: they are flexible guidelines that bend to fit each situation.
p: A principle of management is a broad and general guideline for decision-making and behaviour of managers.
Principles are not techniques: techniques are procedures or methods (a series of steps), while principles guide the choices a manager makes while using techniques.
Principles are not values: values are general rules of behaviour accepted by society, while principles are technical guidelines for managerial action.

Nature: universal applicability, general guidelines, formed by practice and experimentation, flexible, mainly behavioural, show cause-and-effect relationships, and contingent (application depends on the situation).

ex.q: A manager applies 'division of work' strictly in a car factory but only partly in a small design studio. Which feature of principles does this show?
st: The same principle is used in both places.
It is modified to suit the size and nature of each firm.
Principles can be adapted, so they are flexible (and contingent on the situation).

topics.rl: A cricket coach's principle 'keep the batting order stable' is a guideline, not a law. In a tight chase the order may change. Management principles work the same way.

rv.summary: A principle of management is a broad and general guideline for managers' decisions and behaviour. Principles are different from techniques and values, and they are universal, flexible, behavioural and contingent.
focus: Define a principle of management
Distinguish principles from techniques and from values
Identify each feature of the nature of principles from a case
remember: Principle: a broad and general guideline for decision-making and behaviour of managers
Techniques are procedures (a series of steps); principles guide choices while using techniques
Nature: universal, general, formed by practice and experimentation, flexible, mainly behavioural, cause and effect, contingent
traps: Principles are not rigid rules like laws of science: they are flexible
Don't swap the meanings of principles and techniques
Universal does not mean applied in exactly the same way everywhere

topics.h: Why do companies spend lakhs training managers in principles when anyone can learn by trial and error? Because trial and error is expensive!
p: Provide managers with useful insights into reality: they improve knowledge, ability and understanding of managerial situations.
Optimum utilisation of resources and effective administration: they help avoid wastage and limit personal bias in administration.

Scientific decisions: decisions become thoughtful, justifiable and free from bias. Meeting changing environment requirements: e.g. division of work leads to specialisation, which suits changing technology.
Fulfilling social responsibility: e.g. fair remuneration and equity. Management training, education and research: principles form the base of management courses and new techniques.

ex.q: Why does an MBA course begin with principles of management rather than straight case studies?
st: Principles form the core knowledge of management.
They are the base for training, education and research.
Without principles, learners cannot analyse cases logically.
ex.a: Because principles are the basis of management training, education and research

topics.rl: Large Indian companies run 'management trainee' programmes that start with core management principles, showing their role in training and education.

rv.summary: Principles of management give managers useful insights, help use resources well, support scientific decisions, help meet a changing environment, fulfil social responsibility and form the base of management training and research.
focus: List and explain the six points of significance
Identify the significance shown in a given statement
Use examples such as division of work and fair remuneration
remember: Scientific decisions: thoughtful, justifiable and free from bias
Principles form the base of management training, education and research
traps: Don't confuse 'scientific decisions' with 'useful insights into reality'
Principles do not relate only to profit; they also help fulfil social responsibility
Trial and error is not cheaper; principles save that effort

topics.h: In the 1880s an American engineer stood with a stopwatch on a factory floor and asked: 'Is there ONE best way to do this job?' His name was F.W. Taylor.
p: F.W. Taylor (1856-1915) is called the father of scientific management. He defined it as knowing exactly what you want people to do and seeing that they do it in the best and cheapest way.
Science, not rule of thumb: replace guesswork and trial and error with scientific study of work to find the one best way.
Harmony, not discord: management and workers should understand each other; this needs a complete 'mental revolution' on both sides.
Cooperation, not individualism: cooperation between workers and management replaces competition; management should reward workers' suggestions and workers should not strike unreasonably.
Development of each and every person to his or her greatest efficiency and prosperity: scientific selection and training of workers so each reaches full efficiency.

ex.q: At Meghna Steel, managers and workers used to blame each other. Now management shares productivity gains and workers suggest better methods. Which principle is this?
st: The change is in the attitude of both sides.
They now see each other as partners, not rivals.
Such a change of mindset is the mental revolution behind 'harmony, not discord'.

topics.rl: Many Indian factories run 'suggestion schemes' that reward workers for ideas that save cost, an example of Taylor's 'cooperation, not individualism'.

rv.summary: F.W. Taylor, father of scientific management, wanted work done in the best and cheapest way. His principles are science not rule of thumb, harmony not discord, cooperation not individualism, and development of each person.
focus: State Taylor's four principles
Explain mental revolution and link it to harmony, not discord
Identify the principle from a case
remember: Scientific management: knowing exactly what you want people to do and seeing that they do it in the best and cheapest way
Harmony, not discord needs a complete 'mental revolution' on both sides
traps: Don't confuse Taylor with Fayol
Mental revolution belongs to harmony, not discord, not to cooperation
Rule of thumb (guesswork) is not a scientific method

topics.t: Taylor's techniques: functional foremanship and standardisation
topics.h: Imagine eight bosses for one worker, each an expert in one thing! Taylor actually proposed this to make factories better.
p: Functional foremanship: separation of planning from execution (doing). It extends division of work and specialisation to the shop floor. Each worker gets orders from eight specialist foremen.

Under the planning in-charge: instruction card clerk (drafts instructions for workers), route clerk (specifies the route or sequence of production), time and cost clerk (prepares time and cost sheets) and disciplinarian (ensures discipline).

Under the production in-charge: speed boss (timely and accurate completion of jobs), gang boss (keeps machines and tools ready for work), repair boss (keeps machines in proper working condition) and inspector (checks quality of work).
Standardisation of work: setting standards for every business activity, such as process, raw material, time, product, machinery, methods and working conditions.
Simplification of work: eliminating unnecessary diversity of products, i.e. needless varieties, sizes and dimensions. It saves cost of labour, machines and tools, and reduces inventory.

ex.q: A factory makes a bucket in 22 sizes, but 90% of sales come from 5 sizes. Which technique should it use and what is the benefit?
st: Many sizes mean extra moulds, inventory and labour.
Dropping the unnecessary varieties is simplification.
Benefit: lower costs, fuller use of machines and less inventory.

topics.rl: The Bureau of Indian Standards sets standards for products like helmets and cement, which echoes Taylor's idea of standardisation.

rv.summary: Functional foremanship separates planning from doing, with eight specialist foremen over each worker. Standardisation sets standards for every activity, while simplification removes needless varieties, sizes and dimensions.
focus: Name the four foremen under planning and the four under production, with their jobs
Distinguish standardisation from simplification
Explain how functional foremanship extends division of work
remember: Planning in-charge: instruction card clerk, route clerk, time and cost clerk, disciplinarian
Production in-charge: speed boss, gang boss, repair boss, inspector
Simplification: eliminating unnecessary diversity of products
traps: Don't confuse the gang boss (keeps machines and tools ready) with the repair boss (keeps them in working condition)
There are eight foremen, not four
Functional foremanship violates unity of command, not division of work

topics.t: Work study and the differential piece wage system
topics.h: A worker loading bricks bends 40 times an hour. Could the same output come with 25 bends and less tiredness? Taylor's work-study techniques ask exactly that.
p: Method study: finding the one best way of doing a job, from procuring raw material to delivering the product, to cut cost and raise quality.
Motion study: studying the movements of a worker or machine to eliminate unnecessary motions.
Time study: fixing the standard time to complete a well-defined job. It helps decide the number of workers, frame incentive schemes and estimate labour costs.
Fatigue study: deciding the amount and frequency of rest intervals so workers can regain stamina.
Differential piece wage system: two piece rates, a higher rate for workers who reach or exceed the standard output and a lower rate for those below it. Wage = units produced x applicable rate.

ex.q: Standard output is 10 units a day. Rate: ₹50 per unit at or above standard, ₹40 per unit below standard. Asha makes 12 units and Bala makes 8. Find their wages and the difference.
st: Asha reaches the standard: 12 x ₹50 = ₹600
Bala is below the standard: 8 x ₹40 = ₹320
Difference = ₹600 - ₹320 = ₹280

topics.rl: Delivery apps that pay riders more per order after a daily target is crossed use the same idea as Taylor's differential piece wage system.

rv.summary: Work study has four parts: method, motion, time and fatigue study. Taylor's differential piece wage system pays a higher rate to workers who reach the standard output and a lower rate to those below it.
focus: Tell the four work studies apart
Calculate wages under the differential piece wage system
Explain how the system motivates workers
remember: Time study fixes the standard time for a job; fatigue study fixes rest intervals
Wage = units produced x applicable rate
Higher rate if output reaches or exceeds standard; lower rate if below
traps: Don't confuse motion study (movements) with method study (the whole way the job is done)
Don't use the standard output instead of actual output when calculating wages
Don't apply the higher rate to a below-standard worker

topics.t: Fayol's principles (1): division of work to remuneration
topics.h: Henri Fayol ran a French mining company for 30 years and turned his experience into 14 principles still asked in every board exam.
p: Henri Fayol (1841-1925) is the father of general management. He gave 14 principles based on his personal experience.

Division of work: work is divided into small tasks, each done by a trained specialist. Authority and responsibility: there must be a balance (parity) between the two. Discipline: obedience to rules; needs good superiors at all levels, clear and fair agreements and judicious penalties.
Unity of command: an employee should get orders from only one superior. Its violation undermines authority, threatens discipline and creates confusion.

Unity of direction: one head and one plan for each group of activities with the same objective. Unity of command concerns a single employee; unity of direction concerns the whole organisation (or a division).

Subordination of individual interest to general interest: the organisation's interest comes first. Remuneration of employees: pay should be fair and just, allowing a reasonable standard of living within the company's paying capacity.

ex.q: At Nova Foods, a packing worker gets one order from the production manager and an opposite order from the marketing manager. Which principle is violated and what is the effect?
st: The worker has two bosses giving conflicting orders.
One employee should receive orders from only one superior.
Effect: confusion, weak authority and poor discipline.
ex.a: Unity of command is violated, causing confusion

topics.rl: Indian Railways has separate zones, each with its own General Manager and plans for its region, an example of unity of direction.

rv.summary: Henri Fayol, father of general management, gave 14 principles. The first seven are division of work, authority and responsibility, discipline, unity of command, unity of direction, subordination of individual interest and remuneration.
focus: Explain these seven principles with examples
Distinguish unity of command from unity of direction
Identify the principle violated in a case and its effect
remember: Unity of command: an employee should get orders from only one superior
Unity of direction: one head and one plan for each group of activities with the same objective
Authority and responsibility must be balanced (parity)
traps: Don't confuse unity of command (one employee) with unity of direction (whole organisation or division)
Discipline does not mean harsh punishment; penalties must be judicious
Two bosses do not improve control; they create confusion

topics.t: Fayol's principles (2): centralisation to esprit de corps
topics.h: Two managers at the same level in different departments need to talk urgently, but the formal route goes all the way up and down. Fayol had a shortcut: the gang plank.
p: Centralisation and decentralisation: a balance is needed between concentrating decisions at the top and spreading them to lower levels.

Scalar chain: the formal line of authority from the highest to the lowest rank, which communication should follow. Gang plank: in an emergency, employees at the same level (e.g. E and O) may contact each other directly.

Order: 'a place for everything and everyone, and everything and everyone in its place' (material and human order). Equity: kindliness and justice; no discrimination on the basis of caste, religion, sex, language, nationality or other such grounds.
Stability of personnel: employees, once selected and trained, should be kept in their posts long enough to show results; frequent turnover is costly.
Initiative: workers should be encouraged to develop and carry out their plans (e.g. a suggestion system). Esprit de corps: team spirit and unity; the manager should replace 'I' with 'We'.

ex.q: A firm hires and fires sales staff every three months. Which principle is violated and what is a likely consequence?
st: Employees are not kept long enough to settle and perform.
This goes against stability of personnel.
Consequence: high hiring and training costs, low efficiency and insecurity.
ex.a: Stability of personnel; higher costs and lower efficiency

topics.rl: Indian cricket's famous team huddles and 'we win together' talk reflect esprit de corps: union is strength.

rv.summary: Fayol's other principles are centralisation-decentralisation, scalar chain (with gang plank), order, equity, stability of personnel, initiative and esprit de corps.
focus: Explain each of these seven principles
Explain the gang plank and when it is used
Identify the principle violated in a case
remember: Order: 'a place for everything and everyone, and everything and everyone in its place'
Gang plank: in an emergency, employees at the same level may contact each other directly
Esprit de corps: replace 'I' with 'We'
traps: Fayol did not recommend full decentralisation; he asked for a balance
Don't confuse esprit de corps (team spirit) with initiative (own plans, suggestions)
The scalar chain cannot be skipped at any time; the gang plank is for emergencies

topics.t: Fayol versus Taylor and case applications
topics.h: Fayol looked down from the boardroom; Taylor looked up from the shop floor. Same goal of better management, very different lenses.
p: Perspective: Fayol from top management; Taylor from the supervisory (shop floor) level.
Unity of command: Fayol was a staunch supporter; Taylor did not consider it important (functional foremanship gives eight bosses).
Applicability: Fayol's principles are universally applicable; Taylor's apply to specialised situations.
Basis of formation: Fayol used personal experience; Taylor used observation and experimentation.

Focus: Fayol on improving overall administration; Taylor on increasing productivity. Personality: Fayol a practitioner; Taylor a scientist. Expression: Fayol's general theory of administration; Taylor's scientific management.

ex.q: In a case, workers at Sunshine Bottling were timed, given rest breaks and paid more for exceeding the standard. Name the techniques and the thinker.
st: Timing workers = time study
Rest breaks = fatigue study
Higher pay above standard = differential piece wage system
All three are Taylor's techniques of scientific management
ex.a: Time study, fatigue study and differential piece wage system (Taylor)

topics.rl: A modern Indian auto plant uses Taylor-style time studies on its assembly line while its board follows Fayol-style principles of order, equity and esprit de corps.

rv.summary: Fayol worked from the top management view, using personal experience, to improve overall administration. Taylor worked at the shop floor, using observation and experimentation, to raise productivity.
focus: Compare Fayol and Taylor on perspective, unity of command, applicability, basis, focus and personality
Name the techniques and the thinker in a case
Know why Taylor's functional foremanship breaks unity of command
remember: Fayol: general theory of administration; Taylor: scientific management
Fayol's principles are universally applicable; Taylor's apply to specialised situations
traps: Don't swap the basis: Fayol used personal experience, Taylor used experiments
Don't swap the focus: Fayol on administration, Taylor on productivity
A true reason does not always explain the assertion

topics.h: A sudden RBI rate hike, a viral health trend, a new law on plastic: none is in a company's control, yet each can make or break its year.
p: Business environment is the total of all individuals, institutions and other forces that are outside the control of a business enterprise but may affect its performance.

Totality of external forces: it is the sum of everything outside the firm. Specific and general forces: specific forces (investors, customers, competitors, suppliers) affect a firm directly; general forces (economic, social, political, legal, technological) affect all firms indirectly.
Inter-relatedness: the forces are linked, e.g. a health trend raises demand for organic food, which brings new firms and new rules. Dynamic nature: the environment keeps changing.
Uncertainty: future changes are hard to predict, especially in fast-moving fields like IT and fashion. Complexity: many forces act together, making their combined effect hard to understand.
Relativity: the impact differs from country to country and region to region, e.g. demand for a product may be high in one region and low in another.

ex.q: Saree demand is huge in parts of India but small in many other countries. Which feature of business environment does this show?
st: The same product faces different conditions in different places.
So the environment's effect depends on the local context.
This is the relativity of business environment.

topics.rl: When the government cut GST rates on some products, demand rose, competitors cut prices and suppliers raised output: a neat picture of inter-related environmental forces.

rv.summary: Business environment is the total of all individuals, institutions and other forces outside the control of a business that may affect its performance. Its features are totality, specific and general forces, inter-relatedness, dynamic nature, uncertainty, complexity and relativity.
focus: Define business environment
Distinguish specific forces from general forces
Identify each feature from a case
remember: Business environment: the total of all individuals, institutions and other forces outside the control of a business enterprise that may affect its performance
Specific forces (investors, customers, competitors, suppliers) affect a firm directly; general forces affect all firms indirectly
traps: Business environment is external, not internal factors
Don't confuse uncertainty (hard to predict) with complexity (many forces acting together)
Regional difference shows relativity, not dynamic nature

topics.h: The first company to spot India's demand for small, fuel-efficient cars in the 1980s ruled the market for decades. Reading the environment early pays!
p: Enables the firm to identify opportunities and get the first-mover advantage: being early to spot a trend lets a firm lead the market.
Helps identify threats and early warning signals: e.g. news of a strong foreign competitor entering lets a firm prepare.
Helps in tapping useful resources: the environment is the source of finance, machines, raw material and people.
Helps in coping with rapid changes: firms aware of changes can respond quickly. Assists in planning and policy formulation.
Helps in improving performance: firms that continuously monitor the environment perform better.

ex.q: Swastik Tea learns that a global brand will enter India next year. It improves its packaging and widens distribution in advance. Which importance is shown?
st: The news of the new entrant is a threat.
Learning about it early is an early warning signal.
Preparing in advance shows identifying threats and early warning signals.
ex.a: Identification of threats and early warning signals

topics.rl: When digital payments grew after 2016, fintech startups that spotted the opportunity early won a first-mover advantage in UPI apps.

rv.summary: Understanding the business environment helps a firm spot opportunities (first-mover advantage), see threats early, tap resources, cope with change, plan better and improve performance.
focus: List and explain the six points of importance
Distinguish identifying opportunities from identifying threats
Identify the importance shown in a case
remember: First-mover advantage: spotting a trend early lets a firm lead the market
The environment is the source of finance, machines, raw material and people
traps: Don't confuse an opportunity with a threat
A firm cannot control external forces; it can only respond to them
Resources do not come only from inside the firm

topics.h: A festive season boom, a jump in loan interest rates and a new phone that kills the old one: three different dimensions of the same environment.
p: Economic environment: interest rates, inflation, change in people's disposable income, stock market indices and the value of the rupee. E.g. a rise in interest rates makes borrowing costlier for firms and buyers.

Social environment: customs, traditions, values, social trends and society's expectations from business. E.g. festivals like Diwali, Eid and Christmas raise demand; health trends raise demand for organic food; more women working raises demand for ready-to-cook food and creches.

Technological environment: scientific improvements and innovations that offer new ways of producing goods and services and new methods of running a business. E.g. digital watches hurt traditional watchmakers; online platforms changed retail.

ex.q: Classify: (i) the rupee falls against the US dollar; (ii) urban families prefer smaller pack sizes; (iii) UPI replaces cheques for small payments.
st: (i) Value of rupee = economic
(ii) Changing lifestyle and social trend = social
(iii) New method of payment through innovation = technological

topics.rl: When the RBI changes the repo rate, home-loan EMIs move, and so does demand for houses and cars: the economic environment at work.

rv.summary: The economic environment covers interest rates, inflation, income, stock markets and rupee value. The social environment covers customs, values and trends, and the technological environment covers new ways of producing and doing business.
focus: Know the factors in economic, social and technological environment
Classify a given change into the right dimension
Explain how each dimension affects business with examples
remember: Economic: interest rates, inflation, disposable income, stock market indices, value of the rupee
Social: customs, traditions, values, social trends, society's expectations
Technological: scientific improvements and innovations offering new ways of production and business
traps: Not every change in demand is economic: trends and festivals are social
Interest rate changes are economic, not political
A new technology replacing an old product is technological, not social

topics.t: Dimensions: political and legal, and identifying dimensions
topics.h: Investors love a stable country, and tobacco ads must carry a health warning by law. Politics and law shape business too.
p: Political environment: political conditions such as general stability and peace in the country and the specific attitudes of elected government representatives towards business. Stability builds investor confidence.

Legal environment: legislation passed by Parliament, administrative orders issued by government authorities, court judgements and decisions of commissions and agencies. E.g. laws require a statutory health warning on cigarette packs, and advertising of alcoholic drinks is prohibited.

Identifying the dimension: ask what caused the change. Money or prices = economic; habits and values = social; new methods or products = technological; government stability or attitude = political; laws, courts or regulations = legal.

ex.q: A court orders that all food delivery packaging must be compostable within a year. Which dimension, and what should food firms do?
st: A court judgement changes the rules for business.
That is the legal environment.
Firms must plan to switch packaging in time to comply.
ex.a: Legal environment; firms must change packaging to comply

topics.rl: The Consumer Protection Act 2019 and the Companies Act 2013 are both parts of the legal environment of Indian business.

rv.summary: The political environment is about stability and the government's attitude to business, while the legal environment is about laws, orders, court judgements and decisions of agencies. To classify a change, ask what caused it.
focus: Distinguish political from legal environment
Give examples of legal restrictions on business
Classify any change into one of the five dimensions
remember: Political: general stability and peace, and attitudes of elected representatives towards business
Legal: legislation, administrative orders, court judgements, decisions of commissions and agencies
Money or prices = economic; habits = social; new methods = technological; government stability = political; laws or courts = legal
traps: Don't confuse political with legal: laws and court orders are legal
Not every government action is political
A legal restriction is not social just because it concerns values

topics.h: On the night of 8 November 2016, ₹500 and ₹1000 notes ceased to be legal tender. Queues at banks, a rush to digital wallets, and a big lesson in business environment!
p: Demonetisation: the Government of India announced on 8 November 2016 that ₹500 and ₹1000 notes would no longer be legal tender. New ₹500 and ₹2000 notes were issued.

It was a tax administration measure: people holding old notes had to deposit them in banks, bringing hidden cash into the tax net. Those with unaccounted cash had to declare it and pay tax or face scrutiny.
It aimed to curb corruption, counterfeit currency, terrorism financing and black money.
It aimed to channelise savings into the formal financial system, as cash was deposited in banks.
It aimed to create a less-cash (cash-lite) economy by pushing digital payments, leading to more formalisation of the economy.

ex.q: After demonetisation, Raju's tea stall started accepting payments through a QR code. Which feature of demonetisation does this reflect?
st: Cash became scarce for a while.
People and businesses moved to digital modes.
This reflects the aim of creating a less-cash economy.
ex.a: Creating a less-cash economy through digital payments

topics.rl: Small shops across India began displaying UPI and wallet QR codes widely after 2016, showing how a policy change in the economic environment reshaped everyday business.

rv.summary: On 8 November 2016 the Government declared ₹500 and ₹1000 notes no longer legal tender. It aimed to curb black money and fake notes, bring cash into banks and the tax net, and create a less-cash economy.
focus: Recall the date and the notes involved
Explain its features: tax administration, curbing corruption, channelising savings, less-cash economy
Link a case to the right feature
remember: 8 November 2016: ₹500 and ₹1000 notes ceased to be legal tender
New ₹500 and ₹2000 notes were issued
Aim: a less-cash (cash-lite) economy through digital payments
traps: Don't mix up the denominations withdrawn (₹500 and ₹1000) with those issued
Don't confuse demonetisation (2016) with GST (2017)
It aimed at a less-cash economy, not more cash

topics.h: Before a single brick of a metro line is laid, engineers have planned routes, budgets and timelines for years. Planning is thinking before doing.
p: Planning is deciding in advance what to do and how to do it. It bridges the gap between where we are and where we want to go.
Planning focuses on achieving objectives and is the primary function of management: it lays the base for all other functions.
Planning is pervasive (needed at all levels and in all departments, with different scope) and continuous (a plan is made for a period, then a new plan follows).

Planning is futuristic (it looks ahead and forecasts the future), involves decision making (choosing among alternatives) and is a mental exercise (it needs foresight, imagination and sound judgement).

ex.q: Top management at Vega Motors plans a 5-year expansion, while a supervisor plans the next day's shift schedule. Which feature of planning is shown?
st: Planning happens at the top and at the supervisory level.
Only the scope of planning differs between levels.
Planning is needed at all levels: it is pervasive.

topics.rl: The India Meteorological Department's monsoon forecast is a planning premise for farmers, fertiliser firms and tractor makers alike: planning is futuristic.

rv.summary: Planning is deciding in advance what to do and how to do it, bridging where we are and where we want to go. It is the primary function and is goal-focused, pervasive, continuous, futuristic, decision making and a mental exercise.
focus: Define planning
Explain each feature of planning
Identify the feature shown in a case
remember: Planning: deciding in advance what to do and how to do it
Planning is the primary function: it lays the base for all other functions
traps: Don't confuse futuristic (looks ahead) with continuous (one plan follows another)
Primary does not mean only at the top: planning is pervasive
With only one option there is no decision to make

topics.h: A cricket team that has planned its bowling changes doesn't panic when the opponent smashes 20 in an over. Plans calm the chaos.
p: Provides direction: it tells employees in advance what to do and how.
Reduces the risks of uncertainty: managers anticipate changes and plan for them (though risk cannot be eliminated).
Reduces overlapping and wasteful activities: plans coordinate the activities of departments and people.
Promotes innovative ideas: planning is the first function and lets managers think of new ideas.
Facilitates decision making: managers choose the best among alternatives. Establishes standards for controlling: plans give the standards against which actual performance is measured.

ex.q: Without a plan, both the sales and marketing teams of Leela Foods ran separate festive campaigns for the same product. Which importance of planning was missing?
st: Two departments did the same work twice.
Planning would have assigned clear tasks to each.
Planning reduces overlapping and wasteful activities.

topics.rl: Before the monsoon, municipal bodies plan drain cleaning and emergency teams. Planning reduces the risk from uncertain weather, though it can't stop the rain.

rv.summary: Planning provides direction, reduces the risks of uncertainty, cuts overlapping and waste, promotes new ideas, helps decision making and sets standards for controlling.
focus: List and explain the six points of importance
Link planning with controlling through standards
Identify the importance shown in a case
remember: Plans give the standards against which actual performance is measured
Planning reduces risk but cannot eliminate it
traps: Don't say planning removes all risk; it only reduces it
Don't confuse 'provides direction' with 'facilitates decision making'
Planning and controlling are not unrelated

topics.h: Some firms make a perfect 5-year plan, then a pandemic arrives in year one. Plans have limits too.
p: Leads to rigidity: managers may feel they must stick to the plan even when circumstances change.
May not work in a dynamic environment: the environment keeps changing, and plans cannot foresee every change.
Reduces creativity: if middle and lower managers only follow plans made by top management, they get little chance to use initiative.
Involves huge costs: time and money are spent on research, experts and discussions, which may not always justify the benefits.
Is a time-consuming process: there may be little time left for action. Does not guarantee success: a good plan must still be implemented well; success also depends on execution.

ex.q: Rohan Retail spent 6 months and ₹10 lakh on a market study before opening a store, by which time a rival had already opened in the same area. Which limitations are shown?
st: The study took 6 months, leaving no time to act first.
It also cost a large sum.
This shows planning is time-consuming and involves huge costs.

topics.rl: Several firms with rigid annual plans struggled when lockdowns hit in 2020, while those with flexible plans pivoted faster. Planning can lead to rigidity.

rv.summary: Planning has limits: it can cause rigidity, may fail in a dynamic environment, reduces creativity, costs a lot, takes time and does not guarantee success.
focus: List and explain the six limitations
Distinguish rigidity from reduced creativity
Identify the limitation in a case
remember: Rigidity: managers feel they must stick to the plan even when circumstances change
Planning does not guarantee success: it also depends on execution
traps: Don't confuse rigidity (sticking to an outdated plan) with reduced creativity (no chance for initiative)
Don't mix up importance points with limitations
Planning alone does not ensure success

topics.h: A family planning a wedding sets a budget, assumes the guest count, lists venue options, compares them, picks one, books it and keeps checking. That is the planning process!
p: Step 1 Setting objectives: decide what the organisation wants to achieve; objectives flow down to departments.
Step 2 Developing premises: assumptions about the future, e.g. forecasts of demand, interest rates, government policy. All managers should use the same premises.
Step 3 Identifying alternative courses of action. Step 4 Evaluating alternative courses: weigh positive and negative aspects of each in light of objectives.
Step 5 Selecting an alternative: choose the best (most feasible, profitable, with fewest negative consequences), sometimes a combination.
Step 6 Implementing the plan: putting it into action. Step 7 Follow-up action: monitoring whether the plan is being implemented as intended.

ex.q: Uday Agro assumes the monsoon will be normal and fertiliser demand will rise 10% next year. Which step of planning is this?
st: These are assumptions about future conditions.
Assumptions that underlie plans are called premises.
So this is developing premises (step 2).

topics.rl: Before launching a new train service, railways estimate passenger demand (premises), compare route options (alternatives), choose one, start operations and keep monitoring occupancy (follow-up).

rv.summary: The planning process has seven steps: setting objectives, developing premises, identifying alternatives, evaluating them, selecting one, implementing the plan and follow-up action.
focus: Write the seven steps in correct order
Explain premises and why all managers should use the same ones
Identify the step from a case
remember: Order: setting objectives, developing premises, identifying alternatives, evaluating alternatives, selecting an alternative, implementing, follow-up
Premises: assumptions about the future, such as forecasts of demand
traps: Planning starts with setting objectives, not premises
Don't merge identifying and evaluating, or evaluating and selecting, into one step
Follow-up (monitoring) is not the same as implementation

topics.t: Types of plans: single-use, standing, objectives, strategy, policy
topics.h: A company's 'no credit beyond 30 days' policy is used for years, but its Diwali sale plan is used just once. Plans come in different shapes.
p: Single-use plans are made for a one-time event or project that is unlikely to be repeated, e.g. budgets, programmes and projects. Standing plans are used repeatedly for recurring situations, e.g. policies, procedures, methods and rules.

Objectives are the end results which management wants to achieve. They should be expressed in specific terms, be measurable, have a time limit and be stated in quantitative terms where possible, e.g. 'raise sales by 10% in a year'.

Strategy is a comprehensive plan for accomplishing an organisation's objectives. It covers: determining long-term objectives, adopting a particular course of action and allocating resources. It takes the business environment into account.
Policies are general statements that guide thinking or channel energies towards a particular direction, e.g. a recruitment policy or a pricing policy. They leave room for managerial discretion.

ex.q: Classify: (i) 'We aim to achieve a 20% market share by 2028.' (ii) 'We will enter rural markets with low-priced sachets, backed by a ₹50 crore budget.' (iii) 'We recruit only graduates for sales posts.'
st: (i) A specific, measurable end result = objective
(ii) A comprehensive course of action with resource allocation = strategy
(iii) A general statement that guides decisions = policy

topics.rl: When an Indian phone maker decides to fight a global rival with low prices, online-only sales and heavy local marketing, it is framing a strategy.

rv.summary: Single-use plans are for one-time events and standing plans are for recurring situations. Objectives are measurable end results, a strategy is a comprehensive plan to reach them, and policies are general guides that allow discretion.
focus: Distinguish single-use plans from standing plans with examples
Define objectives, strategy and policy
Classify given statements as objective, strategy or policy
remember: Single-use: budgets, programmes, projects; standing: policies, procedures, methods, rules
Objectives: end results, specific, measurable, with a time limit
Strategy: long-term objectives, a particular course of action and allocating resources
traps: A budget is single-use, not reused year after year
Don't confuse policies (with discretion) with rules (no discretion)
Step-by-step lists are procedures, not strategy

topics.t: Procedures, methods, rules, programmes and budgets
topics.h: 'No mobile phones on the shop floor' leaves no choice. 'Steps to claim travel expenses' leaves no doubt. Different plans, different jobs!
p: Procedure: routine steps on how to carry out an activity, in chronological order. It is meant for internal use, e.g. the procedure for granting leave.

Method: the prescribed way or manner in which a task has to be performed, given the objective, e.g. on-the-job or off-the-job training methods. Procedure is a series of steps for an activity; method is the way of doing one step or task.

Rule: a specific statement telling what is to be done or not done. No flexibility or discretion; violation may lead to a penalty, e.g. 'No smoking in the factory'. A policy is a general guide with discretion; a rule is rigid.
Programme: a detailed statement about a project, outlining objectives, policies, procedures, rules, tasks, resources and timing. It combines several plans for a one-time project.
Budget: a statement of expected results expressed in numerical terms, e.g. a sales budget for the year. It is a planning device and also a control device.

ex.q: Classify: (i) 'Wearing a helmet in the plant is compulsory.' (ii) 'Fill form, get it signed by the HOD, submit to accounts.' (iii) 'Sales next year: ₹40 crore.'
st: (i) A specific must-do with no discretion = rule
(ii) Chronological steps = procedure
(iii) Expected results in numbers = budget

topics.rl: The Union Budget is a giant numerical plan of expected income and spending: a budget in the planning sense.

rv.summary: A procedure lists routine steps in order, a method is the way to do one task, a rule says what must or must not be done, a programme sets out all plans for a project, and a budget states expected results in numbers.
focus: Define each of the five plan types with an example
Distinguish procedure from method, and policy from rule
Classify given statements
remember: Rule: no flexibility or discretion; violation may lead to a penalty
Budget: a statement of expected results in numerical terms; a planning and a control device
Procedure is a series of steps for an activity; method is the way of doing one task
traps: Don't swap policy (general guide) and rule (rigid)
Don't confuse procedure with method
A programme is not numerical; a budget is

topics.h: A plan to run a hospital is just paper until someone decides who does surgery, who runs the pharmacy and who reports to whom. That is organising.
p: Organising is the process of identifying and grouping the work to be performed, defining and delegating responsibility and authority, and establishing relationships so that people can work together to achieve objectives.
Step 1 Identification and division of work: the total work is divided into manageable activities as per plans, avoiding duplication.
Step 2 Departmentalisation: similar activities are grouped into departments, units or sections, e.g. by function (production, finance) or by product or territory.
Step 3 Assignment of duties: jobs are allocated to members of each department according to their skills (the right person for the right job).
Step 4 Establishing reporting relationships: each person knows from whom to take orders and to whom to report, creating a hierarchy.

ex.q: A new school's principal lists all tasks, forms academic, sports and admin wings, gives each teacher duties, and decides that wing heads report to her. Name the steps in order.
st: Listing all tasks = identification and division of work
Forming wings = departmentalisation
Giving teachers duties = assignment of duties
Wing heads report to principal = establishing reporting relationships
ex.a: Division of work, departmentalisation, assignment of duties, reporting relationships

topics.rl: A cricket board organises by creating selection, coaching, medical and logistics departments, giving each clear duties and a reporting line.

rv.summary: Organising is identifying and grouping work, defining and delegating authority and responsibility, and setting relationships so people can work together. Its four steps are division of work, departmentalisation, assignment of duties and establishing reporting relationships.
focus: Define organising
Write the four steps of the organising process in order
Identify the step shown in a case
remember: Steps: identification and division of work, departmentalisation, assignment of duties, establishing reporting relationships
Departments may be formed by function, product or territory
traps: The process starts with division of work, not departmentalisation
Don't confuse departmentalisation (grouping) with assignment of duties (allocating jobs to people)
Duties are assigned by skills, not randomly

topics.h: Two companies hire equally talented people. One flourishes, one stumbles. The difference is often how well each is organised.
p: Benefits of specialisation: dividing work leads to repetitive tasks, building skill and expertise.
Clarity in working relationships: clear reporting lines tell people whom to obey and whom to report to.
Optimum utilisation of resources: proper assignment avoids duplication and wastage of resources.
Adaptation to change: structures can be modified to respond to changes in the environment.

Effective administration: clear authority avoids confusion. Development of personnel: delegation lets managers develop subordinates and focus on new ideas. Expansion and growth: organising allows new departments and activities to be added.

ex.q: After clearly assigning tasks, Pixel Prints found that two designers were no longer doing the same poster. Which importance is shown?
st: Duplication of work has stopped.
Resources (designers' time) are no longer wasted.
This is optimum utilisation of resources.

topics.rl: When Indian banks added digital banking departments as UPI grew, their organisation structures adapted to change.

rv.summary: Organising brings specialisation, clear working relationships, optimum use of resources, adaptation to change, effective administration, development of personnel and expansion and growth.
focus: List and explain the seven points of importance
Identify the importance shown in a case
Separate organising from planning activities
remember: Optimum utilisation of resources: proper assignment avoids duplication and wastage
Development of personnel: delegation develops subordinates and frees managers for new ideas
traps: Don't confuse clarity in working relationships with effective administration
Setting objectives is planning, not organising
The structure is not fixed forever; it can adapt to change

topics.t: Organisation structure, span of management and functional structure
topics.h: If one manager can handle 8 people well, how many managers does a team of 64 need? The answer shapes the whole organisation chart.
p: Organisation structure is the framework within which managerial and operating tasks are performed. It specifies relationships between people, work and resources.

Span of management is the number of subordinates that can be effectively managed by a superior. It determines the levels of management: a narrow span gives more levels (a tall structure) and a wide span gives fewer levels (a flat structure).
Functional structure groups jobs of a similar nature by function, e.g. production, purchase, marketing, finance, HR, each under a head reporting to the top.
Suitable when the organisation is large, has diversified activities and operations need a high degree of specialisation.

Advantages: occupational specialisation, better control and coordination within a department, managerial efficiency, minimal duplication (economies of scale), easier training, attention to all functional areas. Disadvantages: less emphasis on overall objectives (functional empires), coordination problems across departments, conflicts of interest, and inflexibility (narrow perspective).

ex.q: A firm has 48 workers. If each supervisor can handle 6 workers and each manager can handle 4 supervisors, how many supervisors and managers are needed?
st: Supervisors = 48 ÷ 6 = 8
Managers = 8 ÷ 4 = 2
So 8 supervisors and 2 managers (a wider span would need fewer of both)

topics.rl: Many single-product firms in India, such as a cement manufacturer, are organised by function: production, sales, finance and HR, each under its own head.

rv.summary: Organisation structure is the framework for tasks, and span of management decides its levels. A functional structure groups jobs by function; it gives specialisation and low duplication but can create functional empires and coordination problems.
focus: Define span of management and link it to levels
Solve span-of-management sums
State when a functional structure suits and its merits and demerits
remember: Span of management: number of subordinates a superior can effectively manage
Narrow span = more levels (tall); wide span = fewer levels (flat)
Number needed = workers / span
traps: Don't reverse the effect of span on levels
Don't mix up functional and divisional advantages
Read sums carefully: give the difference if the question asks for it

topics.t: Divisional structure and comparison with functional
topics.h: A company that makes cosmetics, edible oils and steel tubes can't run them all from one marketing department. Enter the divisional structure.
p: Divisional structure groups activities by product lines (or regions); each division is a separate unit with its own functions (production, marketing, finance) and a divisional manager responsible for profit or loss.
Suitable for firms that make a large variety of products using different productive resources, or for firms that are growing and diversifying.

Advantages: product specialisation develops varied skills in divisional heads and prepares them for higher posts; each division's profit or loss can be measured, which fixes accountability; quick decisions due to autonomy; easy expansion by adding new divisions.

Disadvantages: conflict among divisional heads over funds and resources; higher costs due to duplication of activities across divisions; divisional managers may put their own division's interest above the organisation's.

Comparison: functional is based on functions, divisional on products; functional gives functional specialisation, divisional gives product specialisation; responsibility is hard to fix in functional, easy in divisional; functional has low cost (no duplication), divisional has high cost (duplication); divisional heads get wider training for top jobs; coordination across functions is harder in functional and easier within a divisional unit.

ex.q: Prakriti Ltd makes soaps, juices and cricket bats. Should it use functional or divisional structure? Give one advantage.
st: The products are very different and need different resources.
So each product should have its own unit with its own functions.
Advantage: the profit of each product division can be measured and its head held responsible.
ex.a: Divisional structure; it allows clear accountability for each product's performance

topics.rl: Large Indian conglomerates often have separate divisions for consumer goods, hotels, paper and agri-business, each run by its own head.

rv.summary: A divisional structure groups activities by product lines, each with its own functions and a manager answerable for profit or loss. It suits multi-product firms but duplicates activities and raises costs.
focus: State when divisional structure suits
List its advantages and disadvantages
Compare functional and divisional structures point by point
remember: Functional is based on functions; divisional on products
Divisional: responsibility easy to fix, but high cost due to duplication
traps: Divisional does not suit a single-product firm
Divisional structure does not save money; duplication raises costs
Don't swap the bases of the two structures

topics.h: The org chart says who reports to whom. The lunch table says who actually talks to whom. Both shape how work gets done.
p: Formal organisation: the structure deliberately designed by management, with clearly defined authority, responsibility and relationships. Features: specifies relationships, is a means to achieve objectives, coordinates efforts, is designed by top management, places emphasis on work and rules.

Advantages of formal: easy to fix responsibility, no overlapping, unity of command, easier achievement of goals and stability. Disadvantages: delays due to the scalar chain, ignores social needs (human relationships), and may not recognise creativity and talent.

Informal organisation: a network of social relationships that emerges spontaneously from interaction among employees. Features: originates within the formal organisation, behaviour is shaped by group norms, communication has no fixed direction (grapevine), has no definite structure.

Advantages of informal: faster spread of information and quick feedback, fulfils social needs and sense of belonging, compensates for gaps in the formal structure. Disadvantages: spreads rumours, may resist change, pressure to conform to group norms.

Comparison: formal arises from rules and is deliberately created; informal arises from social interaction and emerges on its own. Formal authority comes from position; informal from personal qualities. Formal follows the scalar chain and is rigid; informal has no fixed path and is flexible. Formal leaders are managers; informal leaders are chosen by the group.

ex.q: Employees at Delta Pharma who play cricket every Sunday share news about a restructuring before the official circular. What is this an example of, and give one risk.
st: The group formed on its own through a shared interest.
Information passed through it faster than the formal channel.
This is informal organisation; a risk is that rumours or distorted news may spread.
ex.a: Informal organisation; it may spread rumours

topics.rl: In many Indian offices, a common 'chai break' group becomes an informal organisation where news, tips and support travel faster than official emails.

rv.summary: Formal organisation is deliberately designed by management with clear authority and rules. Informal organisation emerges on its own from social interaction, with grapevine communication and leaders chosen by the group.
focus: State the features, advantages and disadvantages of each
Compare formal and informal organisation
Identify each from a case
remember: Formal: deliberately designed; authority from position; follows the scalar chain
Informal: emerges spontaneously; authority from personal qualities; no fixed path (grapevine)
traps: Informal groups are not planned by management
Official channels are not always faster; the scalar chain can cause delays
Informal organisation does more than spread rumours: it also meets social needs

topics.h: A manager who tries to do everything herself burns out. A manager who hands over work but stays answerable for results grows a team. That is delegation.
p: Delegation is the downward transfer of authority from a superior to a subordinate. The manager remains accountable for the final outcome.
Authority: the right of an individual to command subordinates and act within the scope of the position. It arises from formal position and flows downward. It can be delegated.
Responsibility: the obligation of a subordinate to properly perform the assigned duty. It arises from the superior-subordinate relationship and flows upward. It cannot be entirely delegated.
Accountability: answerability for the final outcome. It arises from responsibility, flows upward and cannot be delegated at all. Authority should match responsibility.
Importance: effective management (managers focus on important work), employee development, motivation of employees, facilitation of growth, basis of management hierarchy, and better coordination.

ex.q: Sales head Meera gives her deputy authority to approve discounts up to 5%. A wrong discount causes a loss. Who answers to the CEO?
st: Meera delegated authority, so the deputy is responsible to Meera.
But accountability cannot be delegated.
So Meera remains accountable to the CEO for the outcome.
ex.a: Meera remains accountable to the CEO

topics.rl: A school principal delegates exam duty to teachers but still answers to the board if the exam goes wrong: authority can be passed down, accountability stays.

rv.summary: Delegation is the downward transfer of authority from a superior to a subordinate, while the superior stays accountable. Authority flows down, responsibility and accountability flow up.
focus: Explain authority, responsibility and accountability
Know which can be delegated and the direction each flows
List the importance of delegation
remember: Authority can be delegated; responsibility cannot be entirely delegated; accountability cannot be delegated at all
Authority flows downward; responsibility and accountability flow upward
Authority should match responsibility
traps: Don't confuse delegation with decentralisation
Accountability does not move down with authority
Responsibility (duty to perform) is not accountability (answerability for outcome)

topics.h: A pizza chain lets each outlet manager decide local offers and staffing on the spot. Head office keeps only big decisions. That is decentralisation.
p: Decentralisation means delegating decision-making authority systematically to the lowest levels, except that which can be exercised only at central points.
Centralisation keeps decision making with a few at the top. No organisation is fully centralised or fully decentralised: a balance is needed, and it shifts as the firm grows.

Importance: develops initiative among subordinates; develops managerial talent for the future; quick decision making; relief to top management; facilitates growth; better control (performance of each level can be evaluated).

Delegation vs decentralisation: delegation is a compulsory act (no manager can do everything) while decentralisation is an optional policy decision of top management. Delegation keeps more control with the superior; decentralisation gives more freedom. Delegation's scope is narrow (superior and immediate subordinate); decentralisation's scope is wide (extends to the lowest level).
Purpose: delegation reduces the burden on the manager; decentralisation increases the role of subordinates by giving them more autonomy.

ex.q: Swift Couriers lets each branch head decide hiring, local pricing and vendor contracts, while the board decides only on new cities. Is this delegation or decentralisation? Give one benefit.
st: Authority is spread systematically to the lowest levels across the whole firm.
It is a policy decision by top management.
So it is decentralisation; one benefit is quick decision making at branches.
ex.a: Decentralisation; quicker decisions at the branch level

topics.rl: Panchayati Raj institutions bring decision making closer to villages, a public-sector echo of decentralisation.

rv.summary: Decentralisation is delegating decision-making authority systematically to the lowest levels, except what must stay at central points. A balance with centralisation is needed.
focus: Define decentralisation and centralisation
Explain the importance of decentralisation
Distinguish delegation from decentralisation
remember: Delegation is compulsory; decentralisation is an optional policy decision
Delegation: narrow scope; decentralisation: wide scope, to the lowest level
No organisation is fully centralised or fully decentralised
traps: Don't swap the two: managers must delegate, decentralisation is a choice
Full decentralisation is not ideal; a balance is needed
Reducing a manager's burden is delegation's purpose, not decentralisation's

topics.h: A startup with a brilliant idea but the wrong team usually fails. Getting and keeping the right people is the job of staffing.
p: Staffing is filling and keeping filled the positions in the organisation structure. It puts the right person in the right job.

Importance: discovers and obtains competent personnel; ensures higher performance by placing the right person on the right job; ensures continuous survival and growth through succession planning; ensures optimum utilisation of human resources (avoids overmanning and shortage); improves job satisfaction and morale through fair rewards.

Human resource management (HRM) includes specialised activities such as recruitment, job analysis, developing compensation and incentive plans, training and development, maintaining labour relations, handling grievances, providing social security and welfare, and defending the company in lawsuits.
Evolution: from labour welfare officers (trade union era) to personnel management to modern HRM, which treats people as a valuable resource.
Staffing is both a managerial function (every manager performs it) and a part of HRM. Its aspects are recruitment, selection and training.

ex.q: Saathi Hospitals keeps a list of trained deputies ready to replace senior doctors who retire. Which importance of staffing is shown?
st: Replacements are planned in advance.
This keeps the hospital running when key people leave.
It shows continuous survival and growth through succession planning.
ex.a: Continuous survival and growth through succession planning

topics.rl: Large Indian IT firms hire lakhs of freshers through campus drives and train them for months, showing staffing as a full HRM activity.

rv.summary: Staffing is filling and keeping filled the positions in the organisation structure, putting the right person in the right job. It is a function of every manager and also a part of HRM.
focus: Define staffing and explain its importance
List the activities included in HRM
Explain why staffing is every manager's function
remember: Staffing: filling and keeping filled the positions in the organisation structure
Aspects of staffing: recruitment, selection and training
traps: Staffing is not only the HR department's job; every manager performs it
Don't confuse staffing with organising
Optimum use of human resources avoids both overmanning and shortage

topics.h: From 'how many people do we need?' to 'what should we pay them?', staffing is a chain of eight linked steps.
p: Step 1 Estimating manpower requirements: workload analysis finds the number and types of people needed; workforce analysis finds the number and types available. The gap shows over- or under-staffing.
Step 2 Recruitment: searching for prospective employees and stimulating them to apply. Step 3 Selection: choosing the best from the pool of applicants.

Step 4 Placement and orientation: placement means the employee occupying the post for which selected; orientation means introducing the employee to colleagues and familiarising them with rules and policies.
