Step 5 Training and development: improving skills and preparing for growth. Step 6 Performance appraisal: evaluating actual performance against standards.

Step 7 Promotion and career planning: moving to higher positions with more responsibility. Step 8 Compensation: all forms of pay or rewards, direct (wages, salaries, incentives) and indirect (paid leave, insurance).

ex.q: A new accountant at Vedant Ltd is shown her desk, introduced to the team and told about leave rules on her first day. Which step is this?
st: She has joined the post she was selected for: placement.
She is being introduced and familiarised with rules.
This is placement and orientation.

topics.rl: Indian Army recruitment rallies estimate needs, attract candidates, select through tests, train recruits, appraise them and promote them over a career: a full staffing process.

rv.summary: The staffing process has eight steps: estimating manpower requirements, recruitment, selection, placement and orientation, training and development, performance appraisal, promotion and career planning, and compensation.
focus: Write the eight steps in order
Distinguish workload analysis from workforce analysis
Distinguish placement from orientation, and direct from indirect compensation
remember: Workload analysis: people needed; workforce analysis: people available
Shortfall = requirement minus availability
Direct pay: wages, salaries, incentives; indirect: paid leave, insurance
traps: The process starts with estimating manpower, not recruitment
Don't swap workload and workforce analysis
Orientation (introducing to people and rules) is not placement (occupying the post)

topics.h: Before looking outside, a smart company asks: 'Is the right person already sitting in our office?'
p: Recruitment is the process of searching for prospective employees and stimulating them to apply for jobs in the organisation. It is a positive process.

Internal sources: transfers (shifting an employee from one job to another, usually at the same level, without substantial change in responsibility or status) and promotions (shifting to a higher position with more responsibility, status and pay).

Merits: motivates employees (promotion prospects); simplifies selection and placement (candidates are already known); transfer is a training tool and helps adjust surplus or shortage of staff between departments; cheaper than external recruitment.

Limitations: no scope for fresh talent; employees may become lethargic if promotion is assured by seniority; a new enterprise cannot use internal sources; spirit of competition among employees may be hampered; frequent transfers may reduce productivity.

ex.q: Agile Bank has a surplus of clerks in Pune and a shortage in Nashik. What should it do and what is the merit?
st: Shifting staff between branches at the same level is a transfer.
Transfer is an internal source of recruitment.
Merit: it adjusts surplus and shortage of staff without hiring from outside.
ex.a: Transfer staff to Nashik; it adjusts surplus and shortage cheaply

topics.rl: Many Indian banks fill branch manager posts by promoting experienced officers, which motivates staff to perform.

rv.summary: Recruitment is searching for prospective employees and stimulating them to apply; it is a positive process. Internal sources are transfers and promotions, which motivate staff and are cheaper but bring no fresh talent.
focus: Define recruitment and explain why it is positive
Distinguish transfer from promotion
List merits and limitations of internal sources
remember: Transfer: shifting to another job usually at the same level, without substantial change in responsibility or status
Promotion: shifting to a higher position with more responsibility, status and pay
traps: Don't confuse recruitment (positive) with selection (negative)
Campus recruitment is external, not internal
A new enterprise cannot use internal sources

topics.h: From a notice at the factory gate to a job post on a website seen by millions, external recruitment has many doors.
p: Direct recruitment: a notice is placed on the notice board for vacancies; job seekers assemble at the premises. Used for casual or unskilled jobs. Casual callers: a database of unsolicited applications kept in the office.
Advertisement in newspapers and journals: wider choice but may bring a flood of applications. Employment exchanges: government-run, mainly for unskilled and skilled operative jobs.

Placement agencies and management consultants: provide a database of qualified candidates for technical, professional and managerial posts, for a fee. Campus recruitment: firms visit colleges and institutes to hire students.

Recommendations of employees: present employees suggest known people (background known, but risk of favouritism). Labour contractors: supply unskilled workers at short notice. Web publishing: job sites and company websites.
Merits of external sources: qualified personnel, wider choice, fresh talent, competitive spirit among existing staff. Limitations: dissatisfaction among existing employees, lengthy process, costly.

ex.q: Zoom Logistics needs 200 loaders within a week for the festive rush. Which external source suits best, and why?
st: The jobs are unskilled and needed quickly.
Labour contractors can supply unskilled workers at short notice (direct recruitment at the gate is another quick option).
So labour contractors suit best.

topics.rl: India's National Career Service portal and state employment exchanges help connect job seekers with employers, an external source of recruitment.

rv.summary: External sources include direct recruitment, casual callers, advertisement, employment exchanges, placement agencies, campus recruitment, employee recommendations, labour contractors and web publishing. They bring fresh talent but are costly and lengthy.
focus: Match each external source to the type of job it suits
List merits and limitations of external sources
Choose a suitable source in a case
remember: Direct recruitment: notice board, for casual or unskilled jobs
Placement agencies and consultants: technical, professional and managerial posts, for a fee
Labour contractors: unskilled workers at short notice
traps: Don't confuse casual callers (unsolicited applications) with direct recruitment
External hiring is not cheap or quick
Favouritism is a risk of employee recommendations, not advertisements

topics.h: A thousand applicants, ten vacancies. Selection is the art of saying 'no' to 990 people fairly.
p: Selection is the process of identifying and choosing the best person out of the pool of applicants. It is called a negative process because it rejects more candidates than it accepts.
Steps: preliminary screening, selection tests, employment interview, reference and background checks, selection decision, medical examination, job offer and contract of employment.

Tests: intelligence test (mental ability, IQ, reasoning), aptitude test (potential to learn new skills), personality test (emotions, maturity, value system), trade test (existing skills and knowledge for the job) and interest test (pattern of interests).

Recruitment vs selection: recruitment attracts candidates (positive), selection chooses the best (negative). Recruitment comes first; selection follows. Recruitment is simple; selection is complex and lengthy.

ex.q: An applicant for a plumber's post is asked to fix a leaking joint in front of the panel. Which test is this?
st: The test checks skills the person already has.
It is about the actual trade.
So it is a trade test.

topics.rl: UPSC civil services selection involves screening (prelims), tests (mains), an interview and medical checks before the final offer, a long, careful selection process.

rv.summary: Selection is choosing the best person from the pool of applicants; it is a negative process because it rejects more than it accepts. It has a series of steps and uses intelligence, aptitude, personality, trade and interest tests.
focus: Write the steps of selection in order
Identify each selection test from a case
Distinguish recruitment from selection
remember: Steps: screening, tests, interview, reference checks, decision, medical, job offer, contract
Aptitude test: potential to learn; trade test: existing skills
traps: Negative does not mean unfair; it means rejecting more than accepting
Don't confuse aptitude tests with trade tests
The contract of employment, not the job offer, is the last step

topics.h: A bank teaches a new clerk to use its software: training. It sends a branch manager on a leadership course: development. Same goal of growth, different focus.
p: Training: increasing the knowledge and skills of an employee for doing a particular job. It is job-oriented.

Development: growth of an individual in all respects, including personality, maturity and potential. It is career-oriented. Education: increasing the knowledge and understanding of employees in a broader, conceptual sense.

Benefits to the organisation: systematic learning reduces wastage of effort and money; higher productivity; prepares future managers; increased morale and lower absenteeism and turnover; effective response to the changing environment.
Benefits to employees: better career opportunities, higher earnings, fewer accidents (better handling of machines), increased satisfaction and morale.
Induction training helps a new employee settle down quickly by becoming familiar with the people, surroundings, job and business.

ex.q: Is this training or development? (i) Teaching a cashier to use a new billing system. (ii) A mentoring programme to build a manager's leadership and decision skills.
st: (i) A specific job skill = training
(ii) Overall growth for future roles = development

topics.rl: Skill India programmes train workers in specific trades (training), while executive programmes at management institutes aim at managers' overall growth (development).

rv.summary: Training increases knowledge and skills for a particular job, while development is growth of the individual in all respects. Both benefit the firm and the employee; induction helps a new employee settle in.
focus: Distinguish training, development and education
List benefits to the organisation and to employees
Explain induction training
remember: Training is job-oriented; development is career-oriented
Induction training: helps a new employee settle down quickly
traps: Don't reverse the scope: development is wider than training
Training benefits employees too, not only the firm
Induction is not the same as vestibule training

topics.h: Learning to fly a plane? You'd better start in a simulator, not the real cockpit. Choosing the right training method matters.
p: On-the-job methods (learning while doing): apprenticeship programmes (trainee works under a master worker for a long period, for trades like plumbing and electrical work), coaching (superior guides the trainee as a coach, often to prepare a successor), internship training (joint programme of educational institutions and firms, combining theory and practice) and job rotation (shifting the trainee from one department to another).
Off-the-job methods (learning away from the work place): classroom lectures and conferences, films, case study, computer modelling, vestibule training and programmed instruction.
Vestibule training: employees learn on equipment similar to the actual machines in a separate area (a dummy model). Used when equipment is costly or sophisticated, to avoid damage and accidents.
Programmed instruction: information is broken into small, logical units; the learner answers and gets feedback (rewards) at each step. Computer modelling simulates the work environment.

ex.q: A new airline pilot practises emergency landings in a flight simulator. Which method is this, and why is it used?
st: The trainee uses equipment like the real one, but away from the actual job.
Mistakes in a real aircraft would be dangerous and costly.
This is vestibule training (with computer modelling), an off-the-job method.
ex.a: Vestibule training, to avoid costly damage and danger

topics.rl: CA students in India do articleship with practising firms, combining study with real work, much like internship training.

rv.summary: On-the-job methods (apprenticeship, coaching, internship, job rotation) train while doing. Off-the-job methods (lectures, films, case study, computer modelling, vestibule training, programmed instruction) train away from the work place.
focus: Classify each method as on-the-job or off-the-job
Explain vestibule training and when it is used
Identify the method from a case
remember: Vestibule training: learning on equipment similar to actual machines in a separate area
Programmed instruction: small logical units with feedback at each step
traps: Vestibule training is off-the-job, not on-the-job
Don't confuse apprenticeship (trade under a master worker) with coaching (superior guides a trainee)
Internship is a joint programme of institutions and firms, not apprenticeship

topics.h: Plans are ready, teams are formed, people are hired. But nothing moves until someone says 'Let's go!' Directing is the spark that starts the engine.
p: Directing means instructing, guiding, communicating with and inspiring people in the organisation to achieve its objectives.
Characteristics: directing initiates action; takes place at every level of management (pervasive); is a continuous process; and flows from top to bottom (a manager directs subordinates).

Importance: initiates action; integrates employees' efforts towards common goals; is a means of motivation; facilitates implementation of changes (by reducing resistance through communication and motivation); and brings stability and balance in the organisation.
Elements of directing: supervision, motivation, leadership and communication.

ex.q: When Nirmal Foods decided to shift to automated packing, its managers explained the benefits, trained workers and assured job security, so the change went smoothly. Which importance of directing is shown?
st: Workers usually resist change.
Managers used communication and motivation to reduce resistance.
This shows directing facilitates implementation of changes.

topics.rl: A railway station master guiding staff during a festival rush, through instructions, encouragement and quick communication, is directing in action.

rv.summary: Directing means instructing, guiding, communicating with and inspiring people to achieve objectives. It initiates action, is pervasive and continuous, flows from top to bottom, and has four elements: supervision, motivation, leadership and communication.
focus: Define directing and state its characteristics
Explain the importance of directing
Name the four elements of directing
remember: Directing: instructing, guiding, communicating with and inspiring people to achieve objectives
Elements: supervision, motivation, leadership, communication
Directing flows from top to bottom
traps: Don't confuse pervasive (every level) with continuous (throughout the organisation's life)
Recruitment is staffing, not directing
Directing does not stop once work begins

topics.h: A supervisor in a garment unit settles a quarrel, teaches a new stitch and passes a worker's idea to the manager, all before lunch. That is supervision.
p: Principles of directing: maximum individual contribution; harmony of objectives (individual and organisational goals should match); unity of command; appropriateness of direction technique (suited to subordinates' needs and abilities); managerial communication (clear, and understood as intended); use of informal organisation; leadership; and follow-through (checking whether instructions are being implemented).
Supervision means overseeing subordinates at work. Its meaning varies with the level, but it is especially important at the first line (supervisory) level.

Role or importance of a supervisor: maintains day-to-day contact and friendly relations with workers; acts as a link between workers and management (link pin); maintains group unity by settling disputes; ensures work is done as per targets; provides on-the-job training; builds positive attitudes through leadership; and analyses work and gives feedback.

ex.q: Supervisor Imran notices two workers quarrelling over shift timings. He talks to both and settles the matter so the team works well again. Which role is shown?
st: The workers were in conflict.
The supervisor settled their dispute.
This is maintaining group unity.

topics.rl: Station supervisors on Indian Railways guide staff, train new porters and report problems upward, the classic link-pin role of supervision.

rv.summary: The principles of directing guide managers, for example harmony of objectives, unity of command and follow-through. Supervision is overseeing subordinates at work, and the supervisor is a link pin between workers and management.
focus: List and explain the principles of directing
Explain the role and importance of a supervisor
Identify the principle or supervisor role in a case
remember: Harmony of objectives: individual and organisational goals should match
Follow-through: checking whether instructions are being implemented
Supervisor: link between workers and management (link pin)
traps: Don't confuse harmony of objectives with unity of command
Link pin is the supervisor, not a top manager
On-the-job training is also a supervisor's role, not only HR's

topics.t: Motivation: meaning, features, process and importance
topics.h: Why does one salesperson make 50 calls a day and another only 10, with the same salary? The answer is motivation.
p: Motive: an inner state that energises, activates or moves and directs behaviour towards goals. Motivation: the process of stimulating people to action to accomplish desired goals. Motivators: the techniques used to motivate people, e.g. pay, bonus, promotion, recognition.

Features: motivation is an internal feeling; it produces goal-directed behaviour; it can be positive (rewards, promotion) or negative (punishment, stopping increments); it is a complex process because people differ in needs and reactions.
Process: unsatisfied need → tension → drives → search behaviour → satisfied need → reduction of tension.
Importance: improves performance; changes negative or indifferent attitudes to positive ones; reduces employee turnover; reduces absenteeism; helps introduce changes smoothly.

ex.q: Neha wants a promotion. She feels restless, so she joins an evening course and takes on extra projects. After she is promoted, she feels at ease. Map this to the motivation process.
st: Unsatisfied need: promotion
Tension: restlessness
Drive and search behaviour: course and extra projects
Satisfied need: promotion achieved
Reduction of tension: she feels at ease
ex.a: Unsatisfied need → tension → drive → search behaviour → satisfied need → reduced tension

topics.rl: Sales leaderboards and 'employee of the month' boards in Indian retail chains use positive motivation to raise performance.

rv.summary: Motivation is stimulating people to act to reach desired goals. It is an internal feeling, goal-directed, positive or negative, and complex, and it follows the process from unsatisfied need to reduced tension.
focus: Distinguish motive, motivation and motivators
Write the motivation process in order
State the features and importance of motivation
remember: Process: unsatisfied need → tension → drives → search behaviour → satisfied need → reduction of tension
Motive is the inner state; motivators are techniques like pay, bonus, promotion, recognition
traps: Don't confuse motive (inner force) with motivator (technique)
Not all motivation is positive; punishment is negative motivation
Don't skip tension in the process

topics.h: First you need food, then a safe room, then friends, then respect, and finally the chance to become your best self. Maslow arranged our needs like a staircase.
p: Abraham Maslow's need hierarchy has five levels, from lowest to highest: physiological, safety or security, affiliation or belonging (social), esteem, and self-actualisation.

Physiological needs: basic survival needs like food, water, shelter and sleep; met through basic salary. Safety needs: physical and economic security, e.g. job security, stability of income, pension plans.
Affiliation or belonging needs: affection, sense of belonging, acceptance and friendship. Esteem needs: self-respect, autonomy, status, recognition and attention.
Self-actualisation: the highest need, to become what one is capable of becoming, including growth, self-fulfilment and achievement of goals.
Assumptions: behaviour depends on needs; needs are in a hierarchical order; a satisfied need no longer motivates; a person moves to the next higher level only when the lower need is satisfied.

ex.q: Identify the need: (i) Ravi wants a permanent job with a pension. (ii) Priya wants to be named 'Best Designer' at the annual meet. (iii) Arjun wants to start his own research lab to fulfil his potential.
st: (i) Job security and pension = safety needs
(ii) Recognition and status = esteem needs
(iii) Reaching one's full potential = self-actualisation

topics.rl: A daily-wage worker first seeks enough pay for food and shelter (physiological), then a permanent job with a steady income (safety). A top scientist at ISRO may be driven by self-actualisation.

rv.summary: Maslow arranged needs in five levels: physiological, safety, affiliation, esteem and self-actualisation. A satisfied need no longer motivates, and a person moves up only after the lower need is met.
focus: Write the five needs in order from lowest to highest
Identify the need level from a case
State the assumptions of the theory
remember: Order: physiological, safety or security, affiliation or belonging, esteem, self-actualisation
A satisfied need no longer motivates
Self-actualisation: to become what one is capable of becoming
traps: Esteem is not the highest; self-actualisation is
Recognition and status are esteem needs, not social needs
Job security and pension are safety needs, not esteem

topics.h: Money talks, but so does a thank-you, a challenging project and a say in decisions. Smart firms use both kinds of incentives.
p: Financial incentives are direct or indirect monetary rewards: pay and allowances (salary, dearness allowance, increments); productivity-linked wage incentives; bonus (over and above wages); profit sharing; co-partnership or stock option (shares offered to employees at a price lower than the market price); retirement benefits (provident fund, pension, gratuity); perquisites (car, housing, medical aid, children's education).

Non-financial incentives satisfy psychological, social and emotional needs: status (rank of positions); organisational climate (e.g. autonomy, rewarding orientation, concern for employees); career advancement opportunity; job enrichment (more variety, higher knowledge and skills, more autonomy and responsibility in the job); employee recognition programmes; job security; employee participation (e.g. joint management committees, work committees, canteen committees, suggestion programmes); and employee empowerment (more autonomy and powers to subordinates).
Financial incentives mainly satisfy lower-level needs; non-financial incentives mainly satisfy higher-level needs like esteem and self-actualisation.

ex.q: Classify: (i) A company offers its shares to staff at a lower price than the market price. (ii) A worker's job is redesigned to include planning and quality checks, giving her more responsibility.
st: (i) Shares at a concessional price = co-partnership or stock option (financial)
(ii) More variety, skills and autonomy in the job = job enrichment (non-financial)

topics.rl: Many Indian startups give ESOPs (employee stock options) to retain talent, a financial incentive, while also offering flexible roles and recognition, which are non-financial.

rv.summary: Financial incentives are monetary rewards such as pay, bonus, profit sharing, stock options, retirement benefits and perquisites. Non-financial incentives such as status, job enrichment, recognition, participation and empowerment meet psychological and social needs.
focus: Classify incentives as financial or non-financial
Explain stock option, job enrichment, participation and empowerment
Link incentives to need levels
remember: Stock option: shares offered to employees at a price lower than the market price
Job enrichment: more variety, higher skills, more autonomy and responsibility in the job
Financial incentives meet lower-level needs; non-financial meet higher-level needs
traps: Don't confuse stock option with profit sharing
Don't confuse job enrichment with job rotation
Participation (committees) is not the same as empowerment (more powers)

topics.h: One captain barks orders, another discusses field placements, a third lets senior players decide. Three different leadership styles, and each can work in the right setting.
p: Leadership is the process of influencing the behaviour of people by making them strive voluntarily towards achieving organisational goals.

Features: it is an ability to influence others; it tries to bring change in people's behaviour; it shows the interpersonal relation between leader and followers; it is exercised to achieve common goals; it is a continuous process.
Importance: influences behaviour; maintains personal relations and helps followers meet their needs; introduces required changes; handles conflicts; prepares successors through training.

Styles based on use of authority: autocratic or authoritarian (gives orders and expects compliance; decisions centralised; one-way communication; useful for quick decisions or when subordinates need close supervision); democratic or participative (decides in consultation with subordinates; two-way communication; encourages participation); laissez-faire or free-rein (gives subordinates high independence; leader mainly supports; suits competent and responsible subordinates).

ex.q: Identify the style: (i) Captain Rana decides every field placement himself and allows no discussion. (ii) Manager Sana asks her team for ideas before finalising a plan. (iii) Professor Iyer lets her expert researchers set their own goals and methods.
st: (i) Orders with no consultation = autocratic
(ii) Consultation and participation = democratic
(iii) High independence to experts = laissez-faire

topics.rl: In disaster relief, such as during floods, quick autocratic decisions may save lives, while research labs often prefer a free-rein style.

rv.summary: Leadership is influencing people to strive voluntarily towards organisational goals. Based on use of authority, the styles are autocratic, democratic and laissez-faire.
focus: Define leadership and list its features and importance
Explain the three leadership styles
Identify the style from a case
remember: Autocratic: gives orders, expects compliance, one-way communication
Democratic: decides in consultation, two-way communication
Laissez-faire: high independence to competent subordinates
traps: Leadership relies on influence, not force or fear
Don't confuse laissez-faire with democratic: only democratic involves consultation
Autocratic suits quick decisions, not every situation

topics.h: A manager sends a WhatsApp message: 'Meet at 5.' Half the team comes at 5 a.m. Communication is not just sending; it is being understood.
p: Communication is the process of exchange of ideas, views, facts and feelings between two or more persons to create a common understanding.

Elements: sender (conveys the message), message (content of ideas or feelings), encoding (converting the message into words, symbols or gestures), media (the path: face-to-face, phone, email, letter), decoding (converting the symbols back into meaning), receiver (who gets the message), feedback (receiver's response showing the message was understood) and noise (any obstruction or hindrance, e.g. poor phone line, inattention, ambiguous symbols).

Importance: basis of coordination; helps smooth working of the enterprise; basis of decision making; increases managerial efficiency; promotes cooperation and industrial peace; establishes effective leadership; boosts morale and provides motivation.

ex.q: Manager Joseph writes an email to his team in simple Hindi and English; the team reads it, understands it and replies 'Noted, will do'. Identify encoding, media, decoding and feedback.
st: Encoding: putting his ideas into simple Hindi and English words
Media: email
Decoding: the team reading and understanding the words
Feedback: the reply 'Noted, will do'
ex.a: Encoding = writing in words; media = email; decoding = understanding; feedback = reply

topics.rl: In an ISRO mission control room, clear communication of every command, and confirmation that it was received, can decide mission success.

rv.summary: Communication is the exchange of ideas, views, facts and feelings to create a common understanding. Its elements are sender, message, encoding, media, decoding, receiver, feedback and noise.
focus: Define communication and name its elements in order
Identify each element in a case
Explain the importance of communication
remember: Encoding: at the sender's end; decoding: at the receiver's end
Feedback: receiver's response showing the message was understood
Noise: any obstruction or hindrance in communication
traps: Don't confuse encoding with decoding
Communication is not just sending information; it aims at common understanding
Media is the path, not the encoding

topics.h: The official circular says the office will shift next month. But everyone already knew from the lunch-time grapevine last week!
p: Formal communication follows the official chain of command. Vertical: downward (superior to subordinate, e.g. orders, notices, circulars) and upward (subordinate to superior, e.g. leave applications, grievances, suggestions). Horizontal or lateral: between people at the same level in different departments, e.g. production manager and marketing manager.

Formal networks: single chain (from a superior to a subordinate through a chain, one link at a time), wheel (all subordinates communicate through one superior at the centre), circular (each person communicates with neighbours; slow), free flow (everyone communicates with everyone; fast) and inverted V (a subordinate may communicate with the immediate superior and also with the superior's superior, in a limited way).

Informal communication (grapevine) arises from social interaction, without following official channels. Grapevine networks: single strand (each person tells one other in a sequence), gossip (one person tells everyone non-selectively), probability (a person tells others at random) and cluster (a person tells only those he or she trusts).

Formal vs informal: formal follows the scalar chain, is slower, keeps records and is official; informal follows no fixed path, spreads fast, may distort information and has no records. Managers can use the grapevine to spread useful information and get feedback.

ex.q: At Bloom Ltd, every regional manager reports to and receives instructions from the national sales head only; they don't talk to each other. Which network is this?
st: All communication passes through one central person.
The others do not communicate directly with each other.
This is the wheel network.

topics.rl: Office WhatsApp groups often act as a modern grapevine where news spreads faster than any official memo.

rv.summary: Formal communication follows the official chain and can be vertical or horizontal, using networks like single chain, wheel, circular, free flow and inverted V. Informal communication (grapevine) uses single strand, gossip, probability and cluster networks.
focus: Classify communication as downward, upward or horizontal
Identify formal and grapevine networks
Compare formal and informal communication
remember: Wheel: all subordinates communicate through one superior
Circular is slow; free flow is fast
Gossip: one tells everyone; probability: tells others at random; cluster: tells only those trusted
traps: Don't confuse free flow (fastest) with circular (slow)
Don't confuse cluster (trusted people) with gossip (everyone)
Managers cannot and should not ban the grapevine; they can use it

topics.h: The boss says 'This report is quite good.' One worker hears praise, another hears criticism. Somewhere a barrier is hiding.
p: Semantic barriers (problems in encoding and decoding): badly expressed message; symbols or words with different meanings (e.g. 'value' can mean price, worth or importance); faulty translations; unclarified assumptions; technical jargon; misreading body language and gestures.

Psychological or emotional barriers: premature evaluation (judging before hearing fully); lack of attention; loss by transmission and poor retention (information is lost as it passes through many people); distrust between sender and receiver.

Organisational barriers: organisational policy (if it does not support free flow); rules and regulations (rigid, time-consuming routes); status (status-conscious managers keep distance); complexity in organisation structure (more levels cause delay and distortion); lack of organisational facilities (meetings, suggestion boxes, open-door policy).

Personal barriers: fear of challenge to authority (a superior withholds information); lack of confidence of the superior in subordinates; unwillingness to communicate (subordinates fear it may hurt them); lack of proper incentives for communication.

ex.q: A manager tells a new worker to 'check the BOM against the WIP before the QC run'. The worker looks blank. Which barrier is this?
st: The words are technical short forms.
The receiver does not understand them.
This is technical jargon, a semantic barrier.

topics.rl: In many multilingual Indian workplaces, poor translation of circulars between languages leads to confusion, a classic semantic barrier.

rv.summary: Barriers to communication are semantic (encoding and decoding problems), psychological (emotions and attention), organisational (policy, rules, status, structure, facilities) and personal (fear, lack of confidence, unwillingness, lack of incentives).
focus: List the barriers under each of the four heads
Identify the barrier from a case
remember: Semantic: badly expressed message, words with different meanings, faulty translation, assumptions, jargon, body language
Psychological: premature evaluation, lack of attention, loss by transmission, distrust
traps: Status is an organisational barrier, not a personal one
Fear of challenge to authority is a personal barrier, not psychological
Distrust is psychological, not semantic

topics.t: Improving communication and directing case studies
topics.h: Great communicators aren't born; they follow simple habits: think before speaking, listen well and check understanding.
p: Measures to improve communication: clarify the ideas before communicating; communicate according to the needs of the receiver; consult others before communicating; be aware of the language, tone and content of the message; convey things of help and value to the listener; ensure proper feedback; communicate for the present as well as the future; follow up communications; be a good listener.

Case-based questions in directing ask you to identify: an element (supervision, motivation, leadership, communication), a principle of directing, a need level (Maslow), an incentive (financial or non-financial), a leadership style or a communication barrier.
Tip for cases: look for the key clue words, e.g. 'pension' → safety need; 'shares below market price' → stock option; 'consults the team' → democratic; 'jargon' → semantic barrier.

ex.q: Manager Asha notices her team often misunderstands instructions. She now writes clear points, avoids jargon and asks each person to repeat the task. Which measures is she using?
st: Writing clear points: clarify ideas before communicating
Avoiding jargon: communicate according to the receiver's needs
Asking them to repeat the task: ensure proper feedback
ex.a: Clarifying ideas, suiting the receiver and ensuring feedback

topics.rl: Customer-care teams at Indian telecom firms are trained to listen patiently and repeat the customer's complaint before acting, ensuring feedback.

rv.summary: Communication improves when managers clarify ideas, suit the receiver, consult others, watch language and tone, ensure feedback, follow up and listen well. Directing cases are solved by spotting clue words.

Spot clue words in directing case studies

traps: Written messages still need feedback
Don't confuse follow-up with feedback
Listening matters as much as speaking

topics.h: A car's dashboard tells the driver if speed, fuel or engine heat drifts from normal. Controlling is a manager's dashboard.
p: Controlling means ensuring that activities in an organisation are performed as per the plans. It involves comparing actual performance with standards and taking corrective action.
It is a goal-oriented and pervasive function (needed at all levels and in all organisations).
Controlling is both backward-looking (it checks past performance, like a post-mortem) and forward-looking (it improves future performance by correcting deviations).

Importance: accomplishing organisational goals; judging the accuracy of standards; making efficient use of resources; improving employee motivation (employees know in advance on what basis they will be judged); ensuring order and discipline; facilitating coordination in action (all departments work to predetermined standards).

ex.q: Comet Ltd found its standard of 200 calls per salesperson per day was always exceeded easily, so it raised the standard to 240. Which importance of controlling is shown?
st: Comparing actual results showed the standard was too low.
Controlling helped revise the standard.
This shows controlling helps in judging the accuracy of standards.

topics.rl: Indian Railways tracks train punctuality daily against timetables and acts on delays, a clear example of controlling.

rv.summary: Controlling ensures activities are performed as per plans by comparing actual performance with standards and taking corrective action. It is goal-oriented, pervasive, and both backward- and forward-looking.
focus: Define controlling and state its nature
Explain the six points of importance of controlling
Identify the importance in a case
remember: Controlling: comparing actual performance with standards and taking corrective action
Controlling is both backward-looking and forward-looking
traps: Don't say controlling only reviews the past; it also guides the future
Don't confuse controlling with planning
Controlling is not only for top managers; it is pervasive

topics.h: You can count units produced, but how do you measure employee morale or customer goodwill in numbers? Controlling has limits.
p: Difficulty in setting quantitative standards: it is hard to set measurable standards for things like employee morale, job satisfaction and human behaviour, so controlling becomes less effective there.
Little control over external factors: a firm cannot control government policy, technological changes or competition.
Resistance from employees: employees may see control as a restriction on their freedom, e.g. resisting CCTV surveillance.
Costly affair: controlling involves a lot of money, time and effort; small firms may not afford elaborate systems. Benefits should exceed costs.

ex.q: Fine Fabrics installs cameras to monitor workers; workers protest that it invades their privacy. Which limitation of controlling is this?
st: Workers see the cameras as a restriction on their freedom.
They oppose the control system.
This is resistance from employees.

topics.rl: A small kirana store cannot afford costly inventory software that a big retail chain uses: controlling is a costly affair.

rv.summary: Controlling is limited by difficulty in setting quantitative standards, little control over external factors, resistance from employees and its high cost.
focus: List and explain the four limitations
Separate limitations from points of importance
Identify the limitation in a case
remember: Hard to set measurable standards for morale, job satisfaction and human behaviour
Benefits of control should exceed its costs
traps: Don't mix up importance (e.g. judging accuracy of standards) with limitations
Controlling is not costless
Government policy is an external factor, not a problem of standards

topics.h: A school sets a target of 95% attendance, records actual attendance daily, and compares the two each week. That's the start of the controlling process.
p: Step 1 Setting performance standards: standards are criteria against which actual performance is measured. Quantitative standards: cost, output, revenue, time (e.g. produce 1,000 units a day). Qualitative standards: goodwill, motivation, improving customer satisfaction.
Standards should be flexible enough to be modified when required.

Step 2 Measurement of actual performance: performance should be measured objectively and reliably, through personal observation, sample checking or performance reports. Measurement should be in the same units as the standard.

Step 3 Comparing actual performance with standards: reveals the deviation, i.e. the gap between actual and desired results. Deviation = actual − standard; percentage deviation = (deviation ÷ standard) × 100.

ex.q: Standard output is 800 units a week. Actual output is 760 units. Find the deviation and the percentage deviation.
st: Deviation = 760 − 800 = −40 units (a shortfall of 40)
Percentage = 40 ÷ 800 × 100 = 5%
So output is 5% below standard

topics.rl: Airlines in India set on-time performance standards and publish actual figures; comparing the two reveals deviations for corrective action.

rv.summary: The first three steps of controlling are setting performance standards, measuring actual performance and comparing it with standards to find the deviation.
focus: Distinguish quantitative and qualitative standards
Know the methods of measuring performance
Calculate deviation and percentage deviation
remember: Deviation = actual − standard
Percentage deviation = (deviation ÷ standard) × 100
Measure in the same units as the standard
traps: Controlling starts with setting standards, not measurement
Divide by the standard, not by the actual figure
Not every standard is numerical; goodwill is qualitative

topics.t: Analysing deviations and taking corrective action
topics.h: If postage costs rise 15% but labour costs rise 5%, which should worry the manager more? Critical point control gives the answer.
p: Step 4 Analysing deviations: deviations within an acceptable range need no action; significant deviations must be studied for their causes.
Critical point control: managers should focus on key result areas (KRAs) that are critical to success, e.g. a 5% rise in labour cost may matter more than a 15% rise in postal charges.
Management by exception: 'an attempt to control everything results in controlling nothing'. Only significant deviations beyond the permissible limit should be brought to the notice of management.

Step 5 Taking corrective action: e.g. defective material → change quality specifications; defective machinery → repair or replace; obsolete machinery → technology upgrade; defective process → modify the process; poor physical conditions → improve them; ineffective training → modify training; ineffective supervision → change supervision; lack of motivation → introduce new incentives.
If deviations cannot be corrected through managerial action, the standards may have to be revised.

ex.q: Planned production cost is ₹50 per unit with a permissible deviation of 2%. Actual cost is ₹52. Should it be reported under management by exception?
st: Deviation = ₹52 − ₹50 = ₹2
Percentage = 2 ÷ 50 × 100 = 4%
4% exceeds the 2% limit, so it is significant and should be reported to management
ex.a: Yes, the 4% deviation exceeds the 2% limit

topics.rl: A hospital such as AIIMS tracks critical indicators like infection rates closely while allowing minor variations in less critical areas: critical point control in practice.

rv.summary: Step 4 analyses deviations using critical point control and management by exception, and Step 5 takes corrective action suited to the cause. If deviations cannot be corrected, standards may be revised.

Decide whether a deviation must be reported
Match each cause of deviation to its corrective action
remember: Management by exception: 'an attempt to control everything results in controlling nothing'
Critical point control: focus on key result areas (KRAs)
traps: Don't confuse critical point control (KRAs) with management by exception (only significant deviations)
Not every deviation must be reported
A bigger percentage does not always matter more; KRAs matter more

topics.h: Planning without controlling is like setting a GPS destination and never checking the route. Controlling without planning is like checking a route that doesn't exist.
p: Planning and controlling are inseparable twins of management. Planning is the base for controlling, and controlling completes the planning cycle.
Planning without controlling is meaningless, and controlling without planning is blind: without plans there are no standards to control against.
Planning is prescriptive (it prescribes actions), while controlling is evaluative (it evaluates whether decisions were translated into action).

It is usually said that planning is looking ahead and controlling is looking back. But both are actually forward- and backward-looking: planning uses past experience (looking back), and controlling's corrective action improves future performance (looking forward).
Controlling also helps improve future planning by providing information from past performance.

ex.q: A firm made a detailed sales plan but never checked actual sales. What is wrong, using the twins idea?
st: Planning sets targets, but without controlling no one knows whether they are met.
Deviations go unnoticed and uncorrected.
So planning without controlling is meaningless.

topics.rl: The Indian cricket team's analysts plan match strategies and then review match data to fine-tune the next plan, showing planning and controlling feeding each other.

rv.summary: Planning and controlling are inseparable twins: planning gives the standards and controlling completes the cycle. Both look forward and backward.

Explain 'planning is prescriptive, controlling is evaluative'
Show that both are backward- and forward-looking
remember: Planning without controlling is meaningless; controlling without planning is blind
Planning is prescriptive; controlling is evaluative
traps: Don't accept the one-line view that planning only looks ahead and controlling only looks back
Don't reverse the order: plans come first
Planning and controlling are not independent

topics.t: Business finance, financial management and its objective
topics.h: Every rupee in a business is either raised from someone or spent on something. Financial management decides how much, from where and on what.
p: Business finance is the money required for carrying out business activities: to buy fixed assets, run day-to-day operations, modernise and grow.
Financial management is concerned with the optimal procurement as well as the usage of finance. It aims to reduce the cost of funds, keep risk under control and deploy funds effectively.

Role: it decides the size and composition of fixed assets; the quantum of current assets and their break-up into cash, inventory and receivables; the amount of long-term and short-term financing; the break-up of long-term financing into debt and equity; and it affects all items in the profit and loss account (interest, expenses, depreciation).
Objective: wealth maximisation of shareholders, i.e. maximising the market value of equity shares. A financial decision is good if it increases the value of the equity shares.

ex.q: Two projects: A promises quick profits but sharply raises risk; B gives steady returns and is expected to raise the company's share price. Which fits the objective of financial management?
st: The objective is to maximise shareholders' wealth.
Wealth is reflected in the market price of equity shares.
Project B is expected to raise the share price, so it fits better.
ex.a: Project B, as it is expected to increase the market value of shares

topics.rl: When a listed Indian company announces a smart expansion, its share price often rises, reflecting an increase in shareholders' wealth.

rv.summary: Financial management is concerned with the optimal procurement as well as usage of finance. Its objective is wealth maximisation of shareholders, that is, maximising the market value of equity shares.

Explain the role of financial management
State and explain the objective of financial management
remember: Financial management: optimal procurement as well as usage of finance
Objective: wealth maximisation, i.e. maximising the market value of equity shares
A financial decision is good if it increases the value of equity shares
traps: The objective is not profit or sales maximisation
Don't confuse face value with market value
Financial management covers both raising and using funds

topics.h: Should a company spend ₹100 crore on a new plant or on new technology? A wrong choice can haunt it for 20 years.
p: Investment decision is about how the firm's funds are invested in different assets. It can be long-term (capital budgeting) or short-term (working capital decisions).
Capital budgeting decisions involve investing in fixed assets such as a new plant, machinery, or a new product line. They affect the earning capacity of the firm over the long run.
Importance: long-term growth and effects; large amounts of funds involved; risk involved; irreversible decisions (very costly to reverse).

Factors affecting capital budgeting decisions: cash flows of the project (expected receipts and payments over its life); rate of return (expected return and risk); and investment criteria involved (techniques like evaluating the amount of investment, interest rate, cash flows and rate of return).

ex.q: Jaya Pharma is choosing between Project X (expected return 14%) and Project Y (expected return 18%) with similar risk. Which factor guides the choice, and which project should it pick?
st: The projects differ mainly in expected return.
Risk is similar, so the higher return is better.
Rate of return guides the choice: pick Project Y.
ex.a: Project Y, based on the rate of return

topics.rl: When Indian Railways decides to build a new dedicated freight corridor, it is making a huge, long-term, hard-to-reverse investment decision.

rv.summary: The investment decision is about how funds are invested in assets: long-term (capital budgeting) or short-term (working capital). Capital budgeting is important because it is long-term, involves large funds and risk, and is irreversible.

State the factors affecting capital budgeting decisions
Identify an investment decision in a case

Capital budgeting decisions are not routine or easily reversed

topics.h: Borrow from a bank or sell more shares? Debt is cheaper but must be repaid with interest; equity is safer but gives away ownership. That's the financing decision.
p: Financing decision is about the quantum of finance to be raised from various long-term sources: shareholders' funds (equity, retained earnings) and borrowed funds (debt, debentures, loans).
Debt is cheaper (interest is tax-deductible) but riskier, because interest and repayment are fixed obligations. Equity has no fixed obligation, so it is less risky for the firm, but it is costlier.

Factors: cost (cheapest source preferred); risk (debt is riskier for the firm); floatation costs (higher cost makes a source less attractive); cash flow position (strong cash flow allows debt); fixed operating costs (if high, use less debt); control considerations (new equity dilutes control, debt does not); state of capital market (equity is easier to raise in a boom).
Retained earnings have no floatation cost and are part of owners' funds.

ex.q: Mehra Steels already has huge fixed operating costs like rent and salaries. Should it raise more debt? Why?
st: High fixed operating costs already create a fixed burden.
Debt adds fixed interest payments on top.
So it should prefer equity or less debt.
ex.a: Prefer less debt, because fixed operating costs are already high

topics.rl: A promoter-run Indian company often prefers bank loans over issuing new shares so the family does not lose control: a control consideration in financing.

topics.h: A company earns ₹100 crore. Should it pay most of it to shareholders today, or keep it to grow tomorrow? That's the dividend decision.
p: Dividend decision is about how much of the profit is distributed to shareholders as dividend and how much is retained in the business for future use.

Factors (1): amount of earnings (dividends come from current and past earnings); stability of earnings (stable earnings allow higher dividends); stability of dividends (firms prefer stable dividend per share); growth opportunities (growing firms retain more); cash flow position (dividend needs cash).

Factors (2): shareholders' preference (some want regular income); taxation policy (if tax on dividends is higher than on capital gains, lower dividends may be preferred); stock market reaction (an increase in dividend is usually seen as good news); access to capital market (easy access allows higher dividends); legal constraints (Companies Act rules); contractual constraints (loan agreements may restrict dividends).
Identifying the decision in a case: buying assets = investment; choosing between debt and equity = financing; dividend vs retention = dividend.

ex.q: Bright Solar has many profitable expansion opportunities. Should it pay a high dividend or retain more profit? Why?
st: Expansion needs funds.
Retained earnings are a cheap internal source.
So it should retain more and pay lower dividends, because of growth opportunities.
ex.a: Retain more, because of growth opportunities

topics.rl: Mature Indian companies in stable sectors such as utilities often pay steady dividends, while fast-growing tech companies usually retain most of their profits.

topics.h: A family that plans its yearly fees, festivals and savings rarely panics. A company with a financial plan rarely runs out of cash at the worst moment.
p: Financial planning is preparing a financial blueprint of an organisation's future operations. It usually covers 3 to 5 years (long-term) and one year or less (short-term budgets).

Objectives: to ensure availability of funds whenever required (including estimating the time and sources of funds); and to see that the firm does not raise resources unnecessarily (excess funds add cost and may encourage wasteful spending).

Importance: helps forecast what may happen under different situations and face them better; helps avoid business shocks and surprises; helps coordinate business functions like sales and production; reduces waste, duplication and gaps in planning; links the present with the future; links investment and financing decisions; makes evaluation of actual performance easier.

ex.q: Coral Toys raised ₹10 crore when it needed only ₹6 crore. The extra funds sat idle while the company paid interest. Which objective of financial planning was ignored?
st: Funds were raised beyond the requirement.
Idle funds add cost without return.
The objective 'not to raise resources unnecessarily' was ignored.
ex.a: To see that the firm does not raise resources unnecessarily

topics.rl: Before the festive season, Indian retailers plan how much cash and credit they need for extra stock, so funds are available exactly when required.

topics.t: Capital structure and trading on equity
topics.h: Same company, same profit, but changing the mix of debt and equity can nearly double the earnings per share. That's the magic, and the danger, of trading on equity.
p: Capital structure is the mix of owners' funds (equity, retained earnings) and borrowed funds (debt). Debt-equity ratio = Debt ÷ Equity.
Optimal capital structure is the mix of debt and equity that maximises the value of equity shares (and EPS) at acceptable risk.
Financial leverage is the proportion of debt in the capital structure. Trading on equity means using fixed-cost debt to increase the earnings of equity shareholders.
Trading on equity is favourable when Return on Investment (ROI) > cost of debt (rate of interest): EPS rises with more debt. If ROI < cost of debt, more debt lowers EPS.
EPS = (EBIT − Interest − Tax) ÷ Number of equity shares, where EBIT = earnings before interest and tax.

ex.q: Total funds ₹20 lakh; EBIT ₹3 lakh (ROI 15%); interest 10%; tax 30%; shares of ₹10. Compare EPS with no debt and with ₹10 lakh debt.
st: EPS rises because ROI (15%) > cost of debt (10%)
ex.a: EPS rises from ₹1.05 to ₹1.40, so trading on equity is favourable

topics.rl: Many Indian infrastructure companies borrow heavily; when projects earn more than the interest rate, shareholders gain, but when returns fall, EPS drops sharply.

rv.summary: Capital structure is the mix of owners' funds and borrowed funds. Trading on equity uses fixed-cost debt to raise equity shareholders' earnings, and it is favourable only when ROI is greater than the cost of debt.

Calculate debt-equity ratio and EPS
Explain when trading on equity is favourable
remember: Debt-equity ratio = Debt ÷ Equity
EPS = (EBIT − Interest − Tax) ÷ Number of equity shares
Favourable when ROI > cost of debt
traps: Don't divide equity by debt
Don't forget to deduct interest and tax when finding EPS
Borrowing does not always raise EPS; if ROI < cost of debt, EPS falls

topics.t: Factors affecting the choice of capital structure
topics.h: Why does one company borrow heavily and another avoid debt? Fourteen factors shape the choice.
p: Cash flow position: strong cash flows allow more debt. Interest coverage ratio (ICR) = EBIT ÷ Interest; a higher ICR means more capacity for debt. Debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) = (Profit after tax + Depreciation + Interest + Non-cash expenses) ÷ (Preference dividend + Interest + Repayment obligation); a higher DSCR means better ability to service debt.

Return on investment: high ROI allows more debt (trading on equity). Cost of debt: lower interest rates favour debt. Tax rate: a higher tax rate makes debt cheaper (interest is deductible). Cost of equity: more debt raises shareholders' risk and their expected return, so debt can be raised only up to a point.

Floatation costs: issue costs affect choice of source. Risk consideration: total risk = business risk + financial risk; if business risk is high, use less debt. Flexibility: keep some unused borrowing capacity for the future.

Control: equity dilutes control; debt (beyond a point) may bring restrictions from lenders. Regulatory framework: SEBI and lenders' rules. Stock market conditions: equity is easier in a boom. Capital structure of other companies in the industry is a useful guide.

ex.q: A company has EBIT of ₹12 lakh and annual interest of ₹3 lakh. Find its interest coverage ratio and comment.
st: ICR = EBIT ÷ Interest = 12 ÷ 3 = 4 times
EBIT covers interest 4 times
A higher ICR means the firm can safely take more debt
ex.a: ICR = 4 times; the firm has good capacity to service debt

topics.rl: Firms in cyclical industries like airlines, where business risk is high, usually try to keep debt lower than stable businesses such as utilities.

rv.summary: The choice of capital structure depends on cash flow (ICR, DSCR), ROI, cost of debt, tax rate, cost of equity, floatation costs, risk, flexibility, control, regulations, stock market conditions and other firms in the industry.

topics.t: Fixed capital: meaning, importance and factors
topics.h: A steel plant needs thousands of crores in furnaces before making a single sheet; a trading shop mostly needs shelves. Why such a gap? Fixed capital factors!
p: Fixed capital is the investment in long-term (fixed) assets like land, buildings, plant and machinery. Its management is called capital budgeting.
Importance of managing it well: long-term growth and effectiveness; large amounts of funds; high risk; irreversible decisions.

Factors (1): nature of business (a trading concern needs less fixed capital than a manufacturing one); scale of operations (larger scale needs more); choice of technique (capital-intensive needs more, labour-intensive less); technology upgradation (industries where assets become obsolete fast, like computers, need more).

Factors (2): growth prospects (higher growth plans need more); diversification (entering new lines needs more); financing alternatives (leasing reduces the need to buy assets); level of collaboration (sharing facilities, e.g. banks sharing ATMs, reduces the need).

ex.q: Kaveri Bank shares an ATM network with other banks instead of installing its own everywhere. Which factor reduces its fixed capital need?
st: Sharing facilities means fewer own assets are needed.
This is collaboration between firms.
So the level of collaboration reduces fixed capital needs.

topics.rl: Indian Railways' huge investment in tracks and coaches contrasts with an online travel agency's small fixed assets: nature of business decides fixed capital.

rv.summary: Fixed capital is investment in long-term assets like land, buildings and machinery. Its need depends on nature and scale of business, technique, technology upgradation, growth, diversification, financing alternatives and collaboration.

Explain the factors affecting fixed capital requirement
Identify the factor in a case
remember: Management of fixed capital is called capital budgeting
Leasing (financing alternatives) and sharing facilities (collaboration) reduce the need

topics.h: A profitable company can still go bust if it can't pay salaries this month. Working capital is the oxygen of daily operations.
p: Working capital is the investment in current assets (cash, inventory, receivables, short-term investments). Gross working capital = total current assets. Net working capital = current assets − current liabilities.
Operating cycle: the time between buying raw material and realising cash from sales (raw material → work-in-progress → finished goods → debtors → cash). A longer cycle needs more working capital.

Factors (1): nature of business (trading and service firms need less, manufacturing more); scale of operations (larger needs more); business cycle (boom needs more, depression less); seasonal factors (peak season needs more); production cycle (longer cycle needs more).

Factors (2): credit allowed (liberal credit to customers needs more); credit availed (more credit from suppliers needs less); operating efficiency (efficient firms need less); availability of raw material (easy, steady supply needs less stock); growth prospects (more growth needs more); level of competition (higher competition needs more); inflation (rising prices need more).

ex.q: Current assets of Lotus Ltd are ₹45 lakh and current liabilities are ₹27 lakh. Find gross and net working capital.
st: Gross working capital = current assets = ₹45 lakh
Net working capital = ₹45 lakh − ₹27 lakh = ₹18 lakh

topics.rl: Umbrella makers in India need far more working capital before the monsoon than in winter: seasonal factors at work.

rv.summary: Working capital is investment in current assets. Net working capital = current assets − current liabilities, and the need depends on the operating cycle and many factors like nature of business, credit, season and inflation.
focus: Calculate gross and net working capital
Explain the operating cycle
Explain the factors affecting working capital
remember: Gross working capital = total current assets
Net working capital = current assets − current liabilities
Operating cycle: raw material → WIP → finished goods → debtors → cash
traps: Don't confuse credit allowed (needs more) with credit availed (needs less)
A boom needs more working capital, not less
Don't add current liabilities; subtract them

topics.h: Your family's savings in a bank, a company's need for a new factory: a financial market is the bridge between the two.
p: A financial market is a market for the creation and exchange of financial assets. It links savers (households) and investors (businesses).
Its allocative function: it mobilises savings and channels them into the most productive uses. Funds can flow through banks or directly through financial markets.
Money market: a market for short-term funds that deals in monetary assets with a maturity period of up to one year.

Major participants in the money market: the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), commercial banks, non-banking finance companies, state governments, large corporate houses and mutual funds. Transactions are usually large, so small individual investors rarely take part directly.

ex.q: A large company has surplus cash for 3 months and wants to lend it safely. In which market will it operate, and why?
st: The funds are surplus only for 3 months.
Short-term funds of up to one year are dealt with in the money market.
So it will use the money market.
ex.a: Money market, because the funds are short-term (up to one year)

topics.rl: When banks lend to each other overnight or the RBI manages short-term liquidity, they are operating in the money market.

rv.summary: A financial market creates and exchanges financial assets, linking savers and investors and channelling savings into productive uses. The money market deals in short-term funds with a maturity of up to one year.
focus: Define financial market and its allocative function
Define money market and name its major participants
remember: Money market: market for short-term funds, maturity up to one year
Participants: RBI, commercial banks, NBFCs, state governments, large corporate houses, mutual funds
traps: Small individual investors are not the main money market participants
Buying a share is a capital market activity, not money market
A financial market deals in financial assets, not physical goods

topics.t: Capital market and its comparison with money market
topics.h: A metro project needs money for 25 years, a bank needs cash for 25 days. Different needs, different markets.
p: Capital market: the facilities and institutional arrangements through which medium and long-term funds, both debt and equity, are raised and invested.
It consists of development banks, commercial banks and stock exchanges. An ideal capital market makes finance available at reasonable cost.

Participants: capital market includes financial institutions, banks, corporates, foreign investors and ordinary retail investors; money market is mainly RBI, banks, financial institutions and finance companies.
Instruments and outlay: capital market deals in equity shares, debentures, bonds and preference shares, often of small unit value; money market deals in short-term debt instruments needing huge sums.

Duration, liquidity, safety and return: capital market is for medium and long term, is liquid (securities can be sold on stock exchanges) but money market instruments are more liquid; capital market is riskier; capital market offers higher expected returns.

ex.q: Compare: (i) a ₹5,000 investment in shares of a listed company; (ii) a bank lending ₹100 crore to another bank for 7 days. Which market is each?
st: (i) Shares, small outlay, long-term ownership = capital market
(ii) Large sum for a very short period between institutions = money market

topics.rl: When an Indian startup lists on the stock exchange and sells shares to lakhs of retail investors, it taps the capital market.

rv.summary: The capital market is where medium and long-term funds, both debt and equity, are raised and invested. Compared with the money market, it is riskier, less liquid and offers higher expected returns.
focus: Define capital market and its constituents
Compare capital and money markets on participants, instruments, duration, liquidity, safety and return
remember: Capital market: medium and long-term funds, debt and equity
Capital market: development banks, commercial banks, stock exchanges
Money market instruments are more liquid and safer; capital market offers higher expected returns
traps: The capital market is not safer than the money market
Don't reverse the outlay: shares have small unit values, money market instruments need huge sums
Bonds and debentures are capital market instruments

topics.h: When a company sells its shares for the first time, money goes to the company. When you sell those shares to a friend later, the company gets nothing. Two markets!
p: Primary market (new issues market): deals with new securities being issued for the first time. Investors' savings go directly to the company, so it contributes directly to capital formation.
Secondary market (stock market or stock exchange): deals in the purchase and sale of existing securities. It provides liquidity and marketability, and contributes indirectly to capital formation.
Function: primary transfers investible funds from savers to companies; secondary enhances liquidity of existing securities.

Participants: in the primary market the company sells and investors buy; in the secondary market both buyers and sellers are investors. Listing: securities need not be listed for the primary market; only listed securities trade in the secondary market.

Prices: in the primary market the issue price is decided by the company's management; in the secondary market prices are set by demand and supply. Location: the primary market has no fixed geographical location; the secondary market operates through a stock exchange.

ex.q: Ananya buys 100 shares in Riva Ltd's IPO. A year later she sells them to Dev on the stock exchange. Identify the market in each case.
st: Shares issued by the company for the first time = primary market
Existing shares sold between investors = secondary market
ex.a: IPO = primary market; later sale = secondary market

topics.rl: A big Indian IPO raises crores for the company in the primary market; after listing, daily trading in its shares happens in the secondary market.

rv.summary: The primary market deals in new securities issued for the first time and helps capital formation directly. The secondary market (stock exchange) trades existing securities and gives liquidity.
focus: Distinguish primary and secondary markets on function, participants, listing, prices and location
Identify the market in a case
remember: Primary (new issues) market: direct capital formation; issue price set by management
Secondary market: existing securities; prices by demand and supply; only listed securities
traps: Not every share purchase is primary; buying existing shares is secondary
The company does not sell in the secondary market; investors trade with investors
The primary market has no fixed location; it is not inside the stock exchange

topics.h: When the Sensex jumps 1,000 points, news channels go wild. Why does a stock exchange matter so much to the whole economy?
p: Under the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956, a stock exchange is any body of individuals, whether incorporated or not, constituted for assisting, regulating or controlling the business of buying, selling or dealing in securities.

Functions: provides liquidity and marketability to existing securities; pricing of securities (through demand and supply); safety of transactions (it is regulated, so deals are safe); contributes to economic growth (savings are channelled into productive investment through the process of disinvestment and reinvestment).
More functions: spreading of equity cult (encouraging people to invest in shares); providing scope for speculation (in a controlled manner, which adds liquidity).
Stock indices like the Sensex (BSE) and Nifty (NSE) reflect the state of the economy, so the stock exchange is called an economic barometer.

ex.q: A stock exchange ensures investors can sell their shares quickly whenever they need cash. Which function is this?
st: Investors can convert shares into cash.
This gives securities a ready market.
This is providing liquidity and marketability.
ex.a: Providing liquidity and marketability to existing securities

topics.rl: India's two major stock exchanges are the BSE (with the Sensex index) and the NSE (with the Nifty index), both located in Mumbai.

rv.summary: A stock exchange, as defined under the SCRA 1956, assists, regulates or controls dealing in securities. It provides liquidity, pricing, safety, economic growth, equity cult and controlled speculation.
focus: Recall the SCRA 1956 definition
Explain the functions of a stock exchange
Explain why it is called an economic barometer
remember: Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956 defines a stock exchange
Sensex is the BSE index; Nifty is the NSE index
traps: Don't confuse the SCRA 1956 with the SEBI Act, 1992
Prices are set by demand and supply, not by a regulator
Equity cult (popularising share investment) is not speculation

topics.h: In 1990 you got paper share certificates by post weeks after buying. Today shares land in your demat account the next working day. How?
p: Step 1 Selecting a broker: a SEBI-registered broker (member of a stock exchange) is chosen. Step 2 Opening a demat account (with a depository participant) and a trading account; PAN is required.
Step 3 Placing the order: the investor tells the broker what to buy or sell, quantity and price. Step 4 Executing the order: the broker buys or sells on the exchange's online system.
Step 5 Contract note: the broker issues a contract note within 24 hours, giving details such as number of shares, price, date and time, and brokerage.

Step 6 Delivery of shares and payment (settlement): the investor delivers shares (seller) or pays (buyer). India follows a rolling settlement; the cycle is now T+1 (trade day plus one working day). Older editions of the book describe T+2.

Dematerialisation: holding securities in electronic form instead of paper. Depositories: NSDL (National Securities Depository Limited) and CDSL (Central Depository Services (India) Limited). A depository participant (DP), such as a bank or broker, is the depository's agent dealing with investors. Benefits: no risk of loss, theft, forgery or damage of certificates; quick transfer and settlement; lower paperwork; easy nomination.

ex.q: Raj buys 50 shares on Monday. Under T+1 settlement, by which day will the trade normally be settled (assuming no holidays)?
st: T is the trade day: Monday.
T+1 means one working day after the trade.
So settlement happens on Tuesday.

topics.rl: Most Indian investors now open a demat account through a bank or broker app, which acts as the depository participant for NSDL or CDSL.

rv.summary: Trading follows six steps: selecting a broker, opening demat and trading accounts, placing the order, executing it, receiving a contract note and settlement. Shares are held electronically with depositories NSDL and CDSL through DPs.
focus: Write the trading steps in order
Explain T+1 rolling settlement
Explain dematerialisation, depositories and DPs
remember: Contract note is issued within 24 hours
Settlement is now T+1 (trade day plus one working day)
Depositories: NSDL and CDSL
traps: Don't count two days for T+1; T+2 was the older cycle
Depositories are not stock exchanges
Trading starts with selecting a broker, not placing the order

topics.t: Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)
topics.h: In the late 1980s, investors faced price rigging, delays in share delivery and shady issues. India needed a watchdog for its markets. Enter SEBI.
p: SEBI was set up by the Government of India on 12 April 1988 as an interim administrative body. It got statutory status on 30 January 1992 through an ordinance, later replaced by the SEBI Act, 1992.
Reasons for setting up: rapid growth of the capital market and malpractices such as price rigging, unofficial premium on new issues, violation of company law rules and delays in delivery of shares.

Objectives: regulate stock exchanges and the securities industry for orderly functioning; protect the rights and interests of investors and guide and educate them; prevent trading malpractices and balance self-regulation with statutory regulation; regulate and develop a code of conduct and fair practices for intermediaries like brokers and merchant bankers.

Protective functions: prohibit fraudulent and unfair trade practices like price rigging; control insider trading; investor protection and education; promote fair practices. Developmental functions: training of intermediaries; research and publishing information; flexible measures to develop markets (e.g. allowing internet trading through registered brokers).

Regulatory functions: registering brokers, sub-brokers, merchant bankers and mutual funds; regulating takeover bids; levying fees; conducting inquiries and audits of stock exchanges; regulating credit rating agencies.

ex.q: SEBI penalises a director who bought shares using unpublished price-sensitive information before a merger announcement. Which type of function is this?
st: Using inside information to trade is insider trading.
Controlling insider trading protects investors.
This is a protective function.

topics.rl: SEBI runs investor-awareness programmes and online resources for first-time investors, part of its protective role of educating investors.

rv.summary: SEBI was set up on 12 April 1988 and got statutory status on 30 January 1992. It regulates the securities market, protects investors and develops the market through protective, developmental and regulatory functions.
focus: Recall SEBI's key dates and reasons for setting up
State SEBI's objectives
Classify a SEBI action as protective, developmental or regulatory
remember: Set up on 12 April 1988; statutory status on 30 January 1992 (SEBI Act, 1992)
Protective: stop price rigging, control insider trading, investor education
Regulatory: registering brokers, merchant bankers and mutual funds
traps: Don't confuse the year set up (1988) with the year of statutory status (1992)
Training intermediaries is developmental, not regulatory
Controlling insider trading is protective, not regulatory

topics.h: Is a market a crowded mandi, or the millions of people who might buy your app? Modern marketing says it's the people.
p: Market: traditionally, a physical place where buyers and sellers meet. In the modern sense, it is the set of actual and potential buyers of a product or service. A marketer is the person or firm that organises the exchange process (usually the seller).

Marketing (Philip Kotler): a social process by which individuals and groups obtain what they need and want through creating, offering and freely exchanging products and services of value with others. Traditionally it meant just selling; the modern view focuses on satisfying customer needs.

Features: needs and wants (marketing identifies and satisfies them); creating a market offering (product with details of size, quality, price, availability); customer value (benefit greater than cost); exchange mechanism (buying and selling of products for money or other value).
What can be marketed: goods, services, experiences, events, persons, places, properties, organisations, information and ideas.

ex.q: Classify what is being marketed: (i) a tourism ad inviting people to visit Kerala; (ii) a campaign urging people not to waste water; (iii) a music festival in Goa.
st: (i) A destination = place
(ii) A social message = idea
(iii) A planned happening = event

topics.rl: Campaigns that tell people to wash hands or save electricity show that even ideas can be marketed.
