rv.summary: In the modern sense, a market is the set of actual and potential buyers, and a marketer organises the exchange. Marketing is a social process of obtaining needs and wants by creating, offering and freely exchanging products of value.
focus: Define market, marketer and marketing
Explain the features of marketing
Classify what is being marketed
remember: Market (modern): the set of actual and potential buyers of a product or service
Marketing (Kotler): a social process of creating, offering and freely exchanging products and services of value
Can be marketed: goods, services, experiences, events, persons, places, properties, organisations, information, ideas
traps: Don't use only the traditional meaning of market as a place
The marketer is usually the seller, not the buyer
Customer value is benefit greater than cost, not just low price

topics.t: Marketing management and marketing vs selling
topics.h: A salesman pushes whatever is in the warehouse. A marketer first asks what customers want, then makes it. Big difference!
p: Marketing management means planning, organising, directing and controlling activities that facilitate exchanges between a firm and its customers. It is the art and science of choosing target markets and getting, keeping and growing customers by creating, delivering and communicating superior customer value.
Scope: selling is a part of marketing; marketing is a wider concept that includes many activities.
Focus: selling focuses on transfer of ownership (title) from seller to buyer; marketing focuses on satisfying customers' needs.

Emphasis and starting point: selling emphasises the product and starts after production, ending with the sale; marketing emphasises customer needs, starts before production (identifying needs) and continues after the sale.
Strategies: selling uses pushing strategies such as promotion and persuasion; marketing uses integrated marketing (product, price, promotion and place).

ex.q: Neel Electronics studied what students want in a laptop, designed one, priced it right, and kept in touch after the sale. Was it selling or marketing?
st: Work began before production with study of needs.
Contact continued after the sale.
It used the whole marketing mix. So this is marketing.

topics.rl: Indian two-wheeler makers study rural needs before designing sturdy bikes, then offer service camps after sale: marketing, not just selling.

rv.summary: Marketing management is planning, organising, directing and controlling activities that facilitate exchange with customers. Marketing is wider than selling: it starts before production with customer needs and continues after the sale.
focus: Define marketing management
Distinguish marketing from selling on scope, focus, emphasis, starting point and strategies
remember: Selling focuses on transfer of ownership; marketing on satisfying customer needs
Selling uses pushing strategies; marketing uses integrated marketing (product, price, promotion, place)
traps: Don't reverse the scope: selling is a part of marketing
Marketing does not start after production; it starts with identifying needs
Marketing does not end with the sale

topics.h: Make lots cheaply? Make the best product? Push hard? Satisfy needs? Satisfy needs AND protect society? Five philosophies, five eras of business thinking.
p: Production concept: focus on availability and affordability; means: mass production and distribution; ends: profit through volume of production.
Product concept: focus on quality, performance and features; means: product improvement; ends: profit through product quality.
Selling concept: focus on selling existing products; means: aggressive selling and promotion; ends: profit through sales volume.
Marketing concept: focus on customer needs; means: integrated marketing; ends: profit through customer satisfaction. Starting point is the market.

Societal marketing concept: focus on customer needs plus society's long-term well-being; means: integrated marketing plus social concerns; ends: profit through customer satisfaction and social welfare. E.g. avoiding pollution and harmful products.

ex.q: Green Valley Juices uses no added sugar, recyclable bottles and fair prices for farmers, while still meeting customer taste. Which philosophy is this?
st: It satisfies customer needs.
It also cares for health, the environment and farmers.
That is the societal marketing concept.

topics.rl: Indian brands switching to plastic-free packaging and healthier ingredients reflect the societal marketing concept.

rv.summary: The five marketing philosophies are the production, product, selling, marketing and societal marketing concepts. Each differs in its focus, means and ends.
focus: State the focus, means and ends of each concept
Identify the concept from a case
remember: Production: availability and affordability; product: quality and features; selling: aggressive selling
Marketing: customer needs, profit through customer satisfaction
Societal: customer needs plus society's long-term well-being
traps: Don't confuse the product concept (quality) with the production concept (mass production)
The marketing concept is not aggressive selling
Don't stop at the marketing concept when society's welfare is involved

topics.t: Functions of marketing and role of marketing
topics.h: Before a packet of chips reaches your hand, someone researched your taste, designed the pack, fixed the price, ran the ads, and trucked it to your shop.
p: Functions (1): gathering and analysing market information; marketing planning; product designing and development; standardisation (producing goods of predetermined specifications) and grading (classifying products into groups by quality or size, common for farm produce like wheat and cotton).
Functions (2): packaging and labelling; branding; customer support services (after-sales service, handling complaints, credit); pricing of the product.

Functions (3): promotion (informing and persuading customers through advertising, personal selling, sales promotion and publicity); physical distribution; transportation; storage or warehousing (to bridge the gap between production and consumption).
Role of marketing in a firm: it identifies customer needs, guides product development, generates revenue and helps the firm survive and grow.
Role of marketing in the economy: it links producers and consumers, creates demand that supports production and employment, helps raise the standard of living and supports economic growth.

ex.q: A rice exporter sorts rice into 'premium', 'standard' and 'broken' categories based on grain length. Which marketing function is this?
st: The product is being classified into groups.
The basis is quality and size.
This is grading.

topics.rl: Agmark grading of farm products like ghee, spices and pulses helps buyers trust quality across India.

rv.summary: Marketing functions include market information, planning, product design, standardisation and grading, packaging and labelling, branding, customer support, pricing, promotion, physical distribution, transportation and warehousing. Marketing also plays a role in the firm and the economy.
focus: List and explain the functions of marketing
Distinguish standardisation from grading
Explain the role of marketing in a firm and in the economy
remember: Standardisation: producing goods of predetermined specifications
Grading: classifying products into groups by quality or size
Warehousing bridges the gap between production and consumption
traps: Don't confuse standardisation with grading
Don't confuse warehousing with transportation
Marketing does not benefit only one firm; it supports the economy

topics.h: You buy toothpaste without thinking, compare three phones for a week, and travel across town for a rare handmade guitar. Same 'shopping', very different products.
p: Marketing mix is the set of marketing tools that a firm uses to pursue its marketing objectives in the target market. It is popularly called the 4Ps: product, price, place and promotion.
Product means anything of value offered to the market: a bundle of utilities (functional, psychological and social) that satisfies needs.

Consumer products (bought for personal use), by shopping effort: convenience products (bought frequently, immediately, with little effort, e.g. soap, toothpaste, newspapers); shopping products (bought after comparing quality, price and style; durable, higher unit price, e.g. clothes, furniture, footwear); speciality products (unique features; buyers make a special effort; high price, e.g. a rare antique or a designer watch).

Industrial products (used for producing other goods or for business): materials and parts (raw materials, manufactured materials and parts, e.g. iron ore, tyres for a car maker); capital items (installations like factory buildings and machinery, and accessory equipment like hand tools and office equipment); supplies and business services (lubricants, stationery, maintenance and repair, legal advice).

ex.q: Classify: (i) bread bought daily; (ii) a sofa bought after visiting four shops; (iii) a limited-edition painting; (iv) lubricating oil bought by a factory.
st: (i) Frequent, little effort = convenience product
(ii) Compared on price and style = shopping product
(iii) Unique, special effort = speciality product
(iv) Used in running the factory = industrial supplies

topics.rl: A kirana store mainly sells convenience products, while a furniture showroom sells shopping products. A small workshop making handcrafted sitars sells speciality products.

rv.summary: The marketing mix is the 4Ps: product, price, place and promotion. Consumer products are convenience, shopping or speciality; industrial products are materials and parts, capital items, and supplies and business services.
focus: Name the 4Ps
Classify consumer products by shopping effort
Classify industrial products
remember: Product: a bundle of utilities (functional, psychological and social)
Convenience (little effort), shopping (compare before buying), speciality (special effort, unique)
Industrial: materials and parts, capital items, supplies and business services
traps: Don't confuse shopping products with speciality products
Machinery is a capital item, not a supply
Stationery and lubricants are supplies, not capital items

topics.h: You can spot your favourite biscuit from across the shop just by its colour and logo. That's the power of branding and packaging.
p: Brand: a name, term, sign, symbol, design or combination used to identify the products of one seller and differentiate them from competitors. Brand name: the part that can be spoken. Brand mark: the part that can be recognised but not spoken (symbol, design, colour). Trade mark: a brand or part of it given legal protection.

Advantages to marketers: product differentiation, easier advertising and display, differential (premium) pricing, easier launch of new products. To customers: easy identification, assurance of quality, status symbol.

A good brand name is short, easy to pronounce, spell, recognise and remember; suggests the product's benefits; is distinctive; is adaptable to packing and different media; is versatile for new products; can be registered and legally protected; has staying power.

Packaging levels: primary (immediate container, e.g. a bottle), secondary (additional layer, e.g. the cardboard box around the bottle), transportation package (for storage and transport, e.g. a corrugated carton of many boxes). Importance: health and sanitation, self-service outlets, innovation opportunity, product differentiation. Functions: product identification, protection, facilitating use, product promotion.

Label: information about the product on the package. Functions: describe the product and its contents; identify the product or brand; grade products; help in promotion; provide information required by law (e.g. statutory warnings, ingredients, maximum retail price).

ex.q: A shampoo comes in a bottle, placed in a small cardboard box, and 48 boxes are packed in a large carton for shipping. Name each level of packaging.
st: Bottle (immediate container) = primary package
Cardboard box = secondary package
Large carton for shipping = transportation package
ex.a: Bottle: primary; box: secondary; carton: transportation

topics.rl: Packaged food in India must carry details like ingredients and MRP on its label, an example of the legal information function of labelling.

rv.summary: A brand identifies a seller's products and sets them apart; a trade mark is a brand given legal protection. Packaging has primary, secondary and transportation levels, and a label gives information about the product.
focus: Distinguish brand name, brand mark and trade mark
State the advantages of branding and features of a good brand name
Identify the levels and functions of packaging and the functions of a label
remember: Brand name can be spoken; brand mark can be recognised but not spoken
Trade mark: a brand or part of it given legal protection
Packaging: primary (bottle), secondary (box), transportation (carton)
traps: Don't confuse brand name with brand mark
Not every brand is legally protected; only a registered trade mark is
Don't confuse primary with secondary packaging

topics.t: Price and factors affecting price determination
topics.h: Why does a ticket to an India-Pakistan match cost more than a regular league game, and why can't a medicine's price be anything the company wants?
p: Price is the amount of money paid by buyers in consideration of the purchase of a product or service. It is a key factor in competition and in the firm's revenue and profit.
Product cost: total cost (fixed, variable and semi-variable) sets the minimum (floor) price, as the firm must cover costs in the long run.
Utility and demand: the utility to buyers sets the upper limit of price. When demand is inelastic, a firm can charge more; when elastic, it must keep prices lower.
Extent of competition: more competition limits a firm's freedom to set prices. Government and legal regulations: governments may control prices of essential goods to protect consumers.

Pricing objectives (profit maximisation, obtaining market share leadership, surviving in a competitive market, attaining product quality leadership) and marketing methods used (distribution system, quality of salespersons, advertising, packaging, credit and customer services) also affect price.

ex.q: A new cola brand enters a market with two big rivals and sets a price lower than both to win buyers. Which factors affect its price?
st: Strong rivals limit the firm's pricing freedom: extent of competition.
It aims to win customers: pricing objective of gaining market share.
So competition and pricing objectives decide the price.
ex.a: Extent of competition and the pricing objective of market share

topics.rl: The government controls the prices of certain essential medicines in India, showing how legal regulations can limit pricing.

rv.summary: Price is the money paid by buyers for a product. It is affected by product cost (floor), utility and demand (ceiling), competition, government regulation, pricing objectives and marketing methods used.
focus: Define price
Explain the factors affecting price determination
Identify the factors in a case
remember: Product cost sets the minimum (floor) price
Utility to buyers sets the upper limit of price
Inelastic demand allows a higher price; elastic demand needs a lower price
traps: Don't confuse price with cost
Cost sets the floor, not the ceiling
Firms cannot always set prices freely; government may control prices

topics.t: Place: channels of distribution and physical distribution
topics.h: A fresh mango from Ratnagiri reaches a Delhi fruit stall through a chain of traders. Who are these middlemen, and why do they matter?
p: Channels of distribution: firms and individuals who take part in the flow of goods from the producer to the final consumer. Their functions: sorting, accumulation, allocation, assortment, product promotion, negotiation and risk taking.

Direct channel (zero level): manufacturer → customer (e.g. company-owned outlets, door-to-door selling, internet sales). Indirect channels: one level (manufacturer → retailer → customer), two level (manufacturer → wholesaler → retailer → customer), three level (manufacturer → agent → wholesaler → retailer → customer).

Factors in choosing a channel: product-related (perishable or technical products need short channels; industrial products usually direct; high unit value short channels); company characteristics (financial strength, degree of control desired); competitive factors (rivals' channels); market factors (size of market, geographical concentration, quantity purchased); environmental factors (economic conditions, legal constraints).
Physical distribution covers activities that move goods from producers to customers. Components: order processing, transportation, warehousing and inventory control.

ex.q: Classify the channels: (i) Ritu buys sarees directly from a weaver's website. (ii) A biscuit maker sells to wholesalers, who sell to grocers, who sell to buyers.
st: (i) No middlemen = zero level (direct)
(ii) Wholesaler and retailer in between = two level

topics.rl: Indian milk cooperatives collect milk from villages and deliver it to cities fast through short channels, because milk is perishable.

rv.summary: Channels of distribution move goods from producer to consumer and can be direct (zero level) or indirect (one, two or three level). The choice depends on product, company, competitive, market and environmental factors; physical distribution moves the goods.
focus: Identify the level of a channel
Explain the factors in choosing a channel
Name the components of physical distribution
remember: Zero level: manufacturer → customer
Two level: manufacturer → wholesaler → retailer → customer
Physical distribution: order processing, transportation, warehousing, inventory control
traps: Don't count the manufacturer or customer as a level
Perishable products need short channels, not long ones
Industrial goods usually go direct, not through many middlemen

topics.h: A TV ad reaches 10 crore people in a second. A salesperson spends an hour with one buyer. Both are promotion, used for very different jobs.
p: Promotion mix: the combination of promotional tools used by a firm: advertising, personal selling, sales promotion and public relations.

Advertising: a paid, impersonal form of communication through mass media by an identified sponsor. Merits: mass reach, enhances customer satisfaction and confidence, expressiveness, economy (low cost per person). Limitations: less forceful, lack of feedback, inflexibility, low effectiveness due to clutter.

Objections to advertising and answers: adds to cost (but it raises demand, giving economies of scale and lower unit cost); undermines social values (but it informs about new products and the buyer chooses); confuses buyers (but it gives information and a rational buyer compares); encourages sale of inferior products (but quality is relative and no firm survives long by cheating); some ads are in bad taste (but this is a criticism of particular ads, not advertising as a whole).

Personal selling: oral presentation in a conversation with prospective customers to make sales. Features: personal form, development of relationships. Role: for business (effective, flexible, minimises waste, lasting relationships); for customers (helps identify needs, gives latest information and expert advice); for society (converts latent demand, creates employment and careers, product standardisation).

Advertising vs personal selling: impersonal vs personal; same message to all vs message adjusted to each buyer; inflexible vs flexible; reaches masses vs few; low cost per person vs high; no direct feedback vs immediate feedback; uses mass media vs salespeople.

ex.q: A firm selling heavy industrial boilers to 50 large factories must explain technical details and negotiate. Advertising or personal selling? Why?
st: Buyers are few and large.
The product is technical and needs explanation and negotiation.
So personal selling, which is flexible and gives immediate feedback, suits best.

topics.rl: During cricket broadcasts, a 10-second TV ad reaches crores of viewers at a low cost per person: advertising's mass reach and economy.

rv.summary: The promotion mix is advertising, personal selling, sales promotion and public relations. Advertising is paid, impersonal mass communication, while personal selling is an oral, face-to-face presentation that is flexible and gives instant feedback.
focus: Explain merits and limitations of advertising
Answer the objections to advertising
Explain personal selling and compare it with advertising
remember: Advertising: a paid, impersonal form of communication through mass media by an identified sponsor
Personal selling: oral presentation in a conversation with prospective customers to make sales
traps: Advertising is not unpaid
Advertising is not costlier per person; it is economical
Advertising is inflexible; personal selling is flexible

topics.t: Sales promotion, public relations and marketing cases
topics.h: 'Buy one, get one free', scratch cards, free samples at the mall: sales promotion is everywhere during Diwali sales.
p: Sales promotion: short-term incentives to encourage purchase or sale. Merits: attention value; useful in new product launch; synergy with other promotion. Limitations: reflects a crisis if used too often; may spoil the product's image.

Activities: rebate (selling at a reduced price to clear stock), discount (price lower than list price), refund (part of price returned on proof of purchase), product combination (another product given free), quantity gift (extra quantity free), instant draws and assigned gifts (scratch cards), lucky draw, usable benefit (e.g. a holiday voucher on buying goods worth a set amount), full finance at 0% (easy instalments with no interest), sampling (free samples to new customers) and contests.

Public relations (PR): managing communication to build a good image and goodwill with the company's publics (customers, employees, shareholders, government, media). Role: press relations, product publicity, corporate communication, lobbying and counselling.
PR tools: news, speeches, events, publications, corporate identity material (logos, letterheads), public service activities and websites.
Case tips: 'free extra 20%' → quantity gift; 'free toothbrush with toothpaste' → product combination; 'scratch and win' → instant draw; 'press conference to clear a rumour' → public relations.

ex.q: Identify: (i) 'Get 25% extra in every pack'. (ii) 'Buy a mixer and get a free bowl set'. (iii) 'Return the wrapper and get ₹10 back'.
st: (i) Extra quantity at the same price = quantity gift
(ii) A free second product = product combination
(iii) Part of price returned on proof = refund

topics.rl: When a company holds a press conference after a product scare to explain facts and safety tests, it is using public relations to protect its image.

rv.summary: Sales promotion gives short-term incentives such as rebates, discounts, refunds, product combinations and quantity gifts. Public relations manages communication to build a good image and goodwill with the company's publics.
focus: Identify sales promotion activities from offers
State merits and limitations of sales promotion
Explain the role and tools of public relations
remember: 'Free extra 20%' → quantity gift; 'free toothbrush with toothpaste' → product combination
Refund: part of price returned on proof of purchase; rebate: reduced price to clear stock
'Press conference to clear a rumour' → public relations
traps: Don't confuse product combination with quantity gift
Don't confuse rebate with refund
Don't confuse PR (reputation) with sales promotion (offers)

topics.h: A pressure cooker that bursts, a fake 'organic' label, an online order that never arrives: consumers need protection, and smart businesses know it.
p: Consumer protection means protecting consumers from unfair trade practices and providing them with ways to get their complaints redressed. It also covers educating consumers about their rights and responsibilities.

From the consumers' point of view: consumer ignorance (many are unaware of their rights and remedies); unorganised consumers (they are scattered and weak compared to big sellers); widespread exploitation (adulteration, false claims, poor service, overcharging).

From the business point of view: long-term interest of business (satisfied customers bring repeat sales); business uses society's resources (so it must serve society's interests); social responsibility (to customers and other groups); moral justification (it is the right thing to do); government intervention (if business ignores consumers, the government may step in with stricter controls).

ex.q: Kiran's grocery chain gives honest weights and quick refunds. Its owner says, 'Happy customers keep coming back.' Which business reason for consumer protection is this?
st: Satisfied customers return and recommend the store.
This benefits the business over time.
This is the long-term interest of business.

topics.rl: Many Indian e-commerce platforms now offer easy returns and grievance officers, partly to win customer trust and partly because consumer law requires it.

rv.summary: Consumer protection means protecting consumers from unfair trade practices, giving them ways to get complaints redressed and educating them. It is important from both the consumers' and the business point of view.
focus: Define consumer protection
Explain its importance from the consumers' point of view
Explain its importance from the business point of view
remember: Consumers' view: consumer ignorance, unorganised consumers, widespread exploitation
Business view: long-term interest, uses society's resources, social responsibility, moral justification, government intervention
traps: Consumer protection is not only about laws; it includes education
Don't confuse consumer ignorance with unorganised consumers
Consumer protection does not only cost business; it brings repeat sales

topics.t: Consumer Protection Act, 2019: scope and meaning of consumer
topics.h: You buy a phone online, a trader buys 100 phones to resell. Only one of you is a 'consumer' under the law. Who?
p: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 replaced the Consumer Protection Act, 1986. It aims to protect and promote the interests of consumers and to set up authorities for timely and effective settlement of consumer disputes.
Scope: it covers all goods and services (unless specifically exempted), and all modes of transactions including online (e-commerce), offline, teleshopping, direct selling and multi-level marketing.

Consumer (goods): a person who buys goods for a consideration (paid, promised, partly paid or under deferred payment), including any user of such goods with the buyer's approval. A person who buys goods for resale or for a commercial purpose is not a consumer.

Consumer (services): a person who hires or avails of services for a consideration, including any beneficiary of such services with the hirer's approval. A person who avails of services for a commercial purpose is not a consumer.

'Commercial purpose' does not include goods bought or services availed exclusively for earning a livelihood by self-employment. A person who gets goods or services free of cost is not a consumer under the Act.

ex.q: Is each a consumer under the Act? (i) Asha buys a refrigerator for her home. (ii) Raj buys 50 refrigerators to resell in his shop. (iii) Asha's mother uses the refrigerator with Asha's approval.
st: (i) Bought for consideration for personal use = consumer
(ii) Bought for resale = not a consumer
(iii) User with the buyer's approval = consumer

topics.rl: The 2019 Act brought e-commerce under consumer law, so online shoppers in India have the same protection as those buying at a local shop.

rv.summary: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 replaced the 1986 Act and covers all goods, services and modes of transaction, including online. A consumer buys goods or hires services for a consideration, but not for resale or commercial purpose.
focus: State the aim and scope of the Act
Decide whether a person is a consumer under the Act
Explain the self-employment exception to commercial purpose
remember: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 replaced the Consumer Protection Act, 1986
A person who buys goods for resale or commercial purpose is not a consumer
Commercial purpose excludes use exclusively for earning a livelihood by self-employment
traps: Not every buyer is a consumer: resale and commercial purpose are excluded
Online purchases are covered by the Act
A person who gets goods or services free of cost is not a consumer

topics.h: You have a right to know what's in your food, and a responsibility to read the label. Rights and duties go together.
p: Six consumer rights: right to safety (protection against hazardous goods and services); right to be informed (about quality, quantity, potency, purity, standard and price); right to choose (access to a variety of goods at competitive prices); right to be heard (to file complaints and have them considered); right to seek redressal (against unfair trade practices and exploitation); right to consumer education (to acquire knowledge and skills to be an informed consumer).

Responsibilities: be aware of the various goods and services available; buy only standardised goods: ISI mark (industrial and electrical goods), Agmark (agricultural products), FPO (fruit products), Hallmark (gold jewellery); learn about risks and follow instructions; read labels carefully (price, weight, dates).

More responsibilities: assert yourself to get a fair deal; be honest (buy only from legal sources, avoid black-marketing); ask for a cash memo; file a complaint when there is a genuine problem; form consumer societies; respect the environment and avoid waste, littering and pollution.

ex.q: Meena's new electric iron gave her a shock because of faulty wiring. Which right was violated, and which mark should she look for next time?
st: A hazardous product harmed her.
This violates the right to safety.
For electrical goods, she should look for the ISI mark.
ex.a: Right to safety; look for the ISI mark

topics.rl: The BIS Hallmark on gold jewellery assures buyers of purity, supporting the right to be informed and the responsibility to buy standardised goods.

rv.summary: Consumers have six rights: safety, to be informed, to choose, to be heard, to seek redressal and to consumer education. They also have responsibilities like buying standardised goods, reading labels and asking for a cash memo.
focus: List and explain the six consumer rights
Match standard marks to products
List consumer responsibilities
remember: ISI: industrial and electrical goods; Agmark: agricultural products; FPO: fruit products; Hallmark: gold jewellery
Right to safety: protection against hazardous goods and services
traps: Don't confuse Agmark with FPO
Asking for a cash memo is a responsibility, not a right
Don't confuse right to safety with right to be informed

topics.t: Who can file a complaint, against whom, and the redressal machinery
topics.h: If a consumer passes away before filing a complaint about a defective product, can the family still seek justice? The Act says yes.
p: Who can file a complaint: a consumer; any registered (recognised) consumer association; the Central Government or a State Government; one or more consumers on behalf of many consumers having the same interest; the legal heir or legal representative of a deceased consumer; the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA).
Against whom: the seller, manufacturer or dealer of defective goods, or the provider of deficient services (including e-commerce entities, for the transactions they handle).

Three-tier redressal machinery set up under the Act: the District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (District Commission), the State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (State Commission) and the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (National Commission).

Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA): set up under the Act to protect, promote and enforce consumer rights as a class; it can act against unfair trade practices and false or misleading advertisements, order recall of unsafe goods and refunds. The Act also provides for mediation to settle disputes through consumer mediation cells attached to the commissions.

ex.q: Two hundred buyers of the same faulty water purifier want to file one complaint. Can they, and who else could file on their behalf?
st: One or more consumers can file on behalf of many consumers with the same interest.
A registered consumer association can also file.
So yes, a joint (class) complaint is allowed.
ex.a: Yes; one or more consumers on behalf of all, or a registered consumer association

topics.rl: The CCPA has issued guidelines in India against misleading advertisements, showing its role in protecting consumers as a class.

rv.summary: A complaint can be filed by a consumer, a registered consumer association, the Central or State Government, consumers on behalf of many, a legal heir, or the CCPA. The redressal machinery has three tiers: District, State and National Commissions.
focus: List who can file a complaint and against whom
Name the three-tier redressal machinery
Explain the role of the CCPA and mediation
remember: Three tiers: District Commission, State Commission, National Commission
CCPA: protects, promotes and enforces consumer rights as a class
traps: The CCPA is not the highest commission; the National Commission is the top tier
The right to complain does not end with death; the legal heir can file
Many consumers with the same interest need not file separately

topics.h: A ₹30,000 phone complaint and a ₹15 crore housing complaint don't go to the same commission. Jurisdiction depends on the value paid.
p: Pecuniary jurisdiction depends on the value of goods or services paid as consideration.
As stated in the Act and the NCERT book: District Commission up to ₹1 crore; State Commission above ₹1 crore and up to ₹10 crore; National Commission above ₹10 crore.

As revised by the Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction) Rules, 2021 (current practice): District Commission up to ₹50 lakh; State Commission above ₹50 lakh and up to ₹2 crore; National Commission above ₹2 crore.

Appeals: against an order of the District Commission, to the State Commission within 45 days; against an order of the State Commission, to the National Commission within 30 days; against an order of the National Commission, to the Supreme Court within 30 days.

ex.q: Under the 2021 rules, where should a consumer file a complaint about a car worth ₹40 lakh? If unhappy with the order, where and within how many days can she appeal?
st: ₹40 lakh is up to ₹50 lakh, so the District Commission has jurisdiction.
An appeal against a District Commission order goes to the State Commission.
The time limit is 45 days.
ex.a: District Commission; appeal to the State Commission within 45 days

topics.rl: A home-buyer complaining about a delayed flat worth several crores would approach the State or National Commission, depending on the value paid.

rv.summary: Pecuniary jurisdiction depends on the value of goods or services paid. The 2021 Rules, now in force, set the limits at ₹50 lakh (District) and ₹2 crore (State), replacing the Act's original ₹1 crore and ₹10 crore. Appeals have fixed time limits.
focus: Choose the correct commission by value paid under the current 2021 Rules
Know the Act's original limits (as in NCERT) so you do not mix them up with the 2021 Rules
State where and within how many days appeals lie
remember: 2021 Rules (current): District up to ₹50 lakh; State above ₹50 lakh up to ₹2 crore; National above ₹2 crore
Act as originally framed (NCERT): District up to ₹1 crore; State above ₹1 crore up to ₹10 crore; National above ₹10 crore
Appeals: District → State in 45 days; State → National in 30 days; National → Supreme Court in 30 days
traps: Don't use the Act's old limits (₹1 crore, ₹10 crore) when a question asks about the 2021 Rules
Jurisdiction is based on value paid, not compensation claimed
Don't use 30 days for an appeal against a District Commission order; it is 45 days

topics.t: Remedies and the role of consumer organisations
topics.h: Winning a consumer case isn't just about money. A commission can order a defect fixed, a product replaced, a misleading ad corrected, or even dangerous goods pulled off the shelves.
p: Remedies available: remove the defect in goods or deficiency in service; replace the defective product with a new one free of defect; refund the price paid; pay compensation for loss or injury; pay punitive damages in suitable cases; discontinue the unfair or restrictive trade practice; withdraw hazardous goods from sale; issue a corrective advertisement to neutralise a misleading one; pay adequate costs to the party.

Consumer organisations and NGOs: educate the public about consumer rights through training programmes, seminars and workshops; publish periodicals and other material; test products in laboratories and publish results; encourage consumers to protest against exploitation; give legal assistance to consumers; file complaints in consumer commissions on behalf of consumers; take initiative in filing cases in courts in the interest of the general public.
Case approach: identify the right violated (e.g. safety), the responsibility missed (e.g. not taking a cash memo), the correct commission (by value paid), and the suitable remedy.

ex.q: A cosmetics firm advertised that its cream removes all scars in 7 days. It doesn't. The commission orders it to publish a new ad stating the true facts. Which remedy is this?
st: The original ad misled consumers.
The order is to publish an ad that corrects the false claim.
This is a corrective advertisement.

topics.rl: Consumer organisations in India test products, publish comparative reports and help people file complaints in consumer commissions.

rv.summary: Remedies include removing defects, replacement, refund, compensation, punitive damages, stopping unfair practices, withdrawing hazardous goods and corrective advertisement. Consumer organisations educate, test products, give legal help and file complaints.
focus: List the remedies available to consumers
Explain the role of consumer organisations and NGOs
Solve cases: right violated, responsibility missed, commission and remedy
remember: Corrective advertisement neutralises a misleading one
Punitive damages may be awarded in suitable cases
traps: A refund does not fix a misleading ad; a corrective advertisement does
Remedies protect the consumer; they do not punish the consumer
Consumer organisations do not act as courts

qa.q: Which statement best describes management?
qa.a: The process of getting things done through others to achieve goals effectively and efficiently
qa.e: Management works through and with people, and aims at both effectiveness and efficiency.

qa.q: Efficiency in management is mainly concerned with:
qa.a: Doing the work at minimum cost with optimum use of resources
qa.e: Efficiency compares output with input; it is about cost and resources.

qa.q: Kavya Textiles had to deliver an export order by 1 March. It delivered on 1 March but spent ₹2 lakh extra on air freight. The company was:
qa.e: The goal was met on time (effective), but extra cost means resources were not used optimally (not efficient).

qa.q: A plant cut its power bill by 15% but failed to meet its production target for the quarter. This shows:
qa.e: Saving cost is efficiency; missing the target means the goal was not achieved, so it was not effective.

qa.q: Which combination should a manager aim for?
qa.e: Good management balances both: achieving goals on time while keeping costs low.

qa.q: Why is management called a 'process'?
qa.a: Because it is a series of interrelated functions performed by all managers
qa.e: Planning, organising, staffing, directing and controlling are linked functions that together make up the management process.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Effectiveness and efficiency always go together. Reason (R): A task can be finished on time even if more resources are used than needed.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: a firm can be effective without being efficient. R is true and is exactly why A fails.

qa.q: Coach Iqbal's cricket academy spent its full budget on a training camp, and the team won the state trophy as planned. If cost was exactly as budgeted, the academy was:
qa.e: The goal (winning) was met and resources stayed within the planned cost, so both conditions hold.

qa.q: Management is required in a business firm, a hospital and a college. This shows that management is:
qa.e: Being needed in every kind of organisation is the all-pervasive feature.

qa.q: Which is NOT one of the three dimensions of management?
qa.e: The three dimensions are work, people and operations. Competitors are outside the organisation.

qa.q: 'Management is a series of continuous, composite but separate functions.' Which feature does this describe?
qa.e: The functions are repeated again and again, so management is continuous.

qa.q: Fresh Bites Foods changed its menu to millet-based snacks after customers became health-conscious. Which feature of management is highlighted?
qa.e: Adapting to changes in the environment (customer tastes) shows management is dynamic.

qa.q: In which dimension of management would a manager deal with employees' needs and group behaviour?
qa.e: Management of people covers dealing with employees as individuals and as groups.

qa.q: Management converts inputs into desired outputs through a production process. This dimension is:
qa.e: Operations management deals with the production process that turns inputs into outputs.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Management is called an intangible force. Reason (R): Its presence is felt through the results of an organisation, such as targets being met and employees being satisfied.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Management cannot be seen; we infer it from its effects, which is exactly what R says.

qa.q: Employees of a firm have different backgrounds and needs, but management makes them work together for common goals. This shows management is a:
qa.e: Management works through a group of people with different needs towards common organisational goals.

qa.q: Which of these is an organisational objective of management?
qa.e: Survival, profit and growth are the organisational objectives.

qa.q: A company employs people from economically weaker sections and plants trees around its factory. This reflects:
qa.e: Creating benefit for society is a social objective.

qa.q: Which need of employees is met by personal growth and development opportunities?
qa.e: Personal objectives include financial, social and higher-level needs; growth is a higher-level need.

qa.q: 'Profit' is important for a business mainly because it:
qa.a: Covers costs and risks and rewards the owners
qa.e: Survival only covers costs; profit goes further to cover risks and reward owners.

qa.q: Management helps people adapt to changes in the environment. This importance is called:
qa.e: Helping the organisation and its people adjust to change creates a dynamic organisation.

qa.q: By reducing costs and raising productivity through better planning, management:
qa.e: Lower costs and higher productivity mean better efficiency.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Management helps in achieving personal objectives of employees. Reason (R): Through motivation and leadership, managers help individuals achieve their goals while contributing to organisational goals.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, and R explains how management helps employees achieve personal goals.

qa.q: Which is an example of the 'development of society' importance of management?
qa.a: Producing good quality products at fair prices and creating jobs
qa.e: Management benefits society through better products, employment and new technology.

qa.q: Management is called an inexact science because:
qa.a: It deals with human behaviour, so its principles must be modified to suit situations
qa.e: Principles exist and are tested, but people behave differently, so results are not exact.

qa.q: Which feature of art does management satisfy when two managers apply the same principles in different styles?
qa.e: Applying the same knowledge in one's own style is personalised application, a feature of art.

qa.q: Which feature of a profession does management clearly satisfy?
qa.e: Management knowledge is well defined and taught; the other features are not fully met.

qa.q: Anyone can be appointed a manager irrespective of qualification. Which feature of a profession does management NOT meet?
qa.e: A profession restricts entry through an exam or degree; management does not.

qa.q: 'Principles of management are developed after repeated observation and testing in different organisations.' This shows management as a:
qa.e: Principles based on experimentation and observation are a feature of science.

qa.q: What is the correct conclusion about the nature of management?
qa.a: It has features of an art and an inexact science, and some features of a profession
qa.e: Management meets all features of art, most of science (inexact) and only some of a profession.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Management is a full-fledged profession. Reason (R): Management has a well-defined body of knowledge.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false because management lacks restricted entry and a binding code. R is true but having knowledge alone does not make it a profession.

qa.q: Manager Nisha keeps improving her handling of team conflicts through years of practice and fresh ideas. This reflects which feature of art?
qa.e: Art improves with practice and creative use of knowledge.

qa.q: Who is responsible for the welfare and survival of the organisation?
qa.e: Top management sets overall goals and is accountable for the organisation's survival.

qa.q: Interpreting the policies framed by top management is a function of:
qa.e: Middle management translates top-level policies into departmental plans.

qa.q: Which level of management directly oversees the efforts of the workforce?
qa.e: Foremen and supervisors interact directly with workers.

qa.q: Mr Rao, Production Head of Sunrise Motors, ensures his department has enough staff and coordinates with the marketing department. He belongs to:
qa.e: Ensuring staff and cooperating with other departments are middle management functions.

qa.q: Ms Fatima, a supervisor at a garment unit, reports workers' grievances to the production manager. This shows the supervisory level acts as a link between:
qa.e: Supervisors communicate workers' problems upward, linking management with workers.

qa.q: Which of these is a top management function?
qa.a: Formulating overall organisational goals and strategies
qa.e: Overall goals and strategies are set at the top.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Supervisory management plays an important role in reducing wastage of materials. Reason (R): Supervisors directly oversee workers and the quality of output.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Because supervisors watch the work closely, they can control quality and wastage. R explains A.

qa.q: Middle management is the link between:
qa.e: Middle managers pass policies down and feedback up between top and supervisory levels.

qa.q: Which function involves deciding in advance what to do and how to do it?
qa.e: Planning sets objectives and the course of action in advance.

qa.q: Grouping tasks into departments and allocating resources is part of:
qa.e: Organising arranges tasks, departments, resources and authority relationships.

qa.q: Ishaan Pharma selects 20 new sales trainees and trains them for a month. Which function is this?
qa.e: Recruiting, selecting and training people is staffing.

qa.q: A manager guides, motivates and communicates with her team to get work done. This is:
qa.e: Leading, motivating and communicating are elements of directing.

qa.q: Which function compares actual performance with standards and takes corrective action?
qa.e: Controlling monitors results and corrects deviations.

qa.q: Which is the correct usual sequence of management functions?
qa.e: Plans come first, then structure, people, guidance and finally checking.

qa.q: Rhea Foods found that actual output was 8% below target and so added a second shift. The function shown is:
qa.e: Finding a shortfall against the target and taking corrective action is controlling.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Planning is considered the first function of management. Reason (R): All other functions are performed within the framework of the plans laid down.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Organising, staffing, directing and controlling all depend on plans, which is why planning comes first.

qa.q: Coordination is best described as:
qa.a: The force that binds all the other functions of management
qa.e: Coordination runs through all functions and binds them together.

qa.q: 'Coordination does not happen automatically; even cooperative employees need it.' This shows coordination is:
qa.e: Managers must make conscious efforts to coordinate; cooperation alone is not enough.

qa.q: Why is coordination called the essence of management?
qa.a: Because it is needed in all functions and at all levels of management
qa.e: Every function and level requires coordination, making it the essence.

qa.q: As Tara Tech grew from 50 to 5,000 employees across five cities, harmonising everyone's efforts became harder. Which reason for the importance of coordination is this?
qa.e: A bigger organisation has more people and units to integrate.

qa.q: The finance department wants to cut costs while the marketing department wants a bigger advertising budget. Which reason for coordination is shown?
qa.e: Separate departments may pursue their own objectives, so coordination is needed.

qa.q: Specialists such as IT experts and lawyers often believe only they know how their work should be done. This creates a need for coordination due to:
qa.e: Specialists focus on their own field and must be integrated with others.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Coordination is the responsibility of all managers. Reason (R): Coordination is needed only at the top level, where overall policies are made.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true: managers at every level coordinate. R is false because coordination is needed at all levels, not just the top.

qa.q: Which is NOT a characteristic of coordination?
qa.e: Coordination is continuous, not a one-time activity.

qa.q: Principles of management are best described as:
qa.a: Broad and general guidelines for managerial decision-making and behaviour
qa.e: Principles guide managers but leave room for judgement.

qa.q: How do principles differ from techniques?
qa.a: Techniques are procedures or methods; principles guide decisions while using techniques
qa.e: Techniques involve a series of steps; principles help in choosing and using them.

qa.q: Principles of management are mainly behavioural because:
qa.a: They aim to influence the behaviour of human beings
qa.e: Management works through people, so its principles target human behaviour.

qa.q: 'If workers are treated fairly, they will be more loyal.' This shows which nature of principles?
qa.e: The statement links a cause (fair treatment) to an effect (loyalty).

qa.q: Management principles are developed through:
qa.a: Practice, experience and experimentation by managers
qa.e: Principles are derived from observation, experience and experiments.

qa.q: The extent to which a principle is applied depends on the situation. This is called:
qa.e: Contingent means its use depends on the prevailing conditions.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Principles of management are flexible. Reason (R): They can be modified by managers to suit the requirements of a situation.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true, and R is the meaning of flexibility.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Principles of management are universally applicable in exactly the same way in all organisations. Reason (R): Principles of management are contingent on the situation.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: Principles apply in all organisations, but not in exactly the same way, because their application depends on the situation. So A is false and R is true.

qa.q: Principles of management help managers make decisions that are logical, justifiable and free from personal bias. This is:
qa.e: Unbiased, reasoned decisions are called scientific decisions.

qa.q: Principles of management form the basis of management courses and help develop new techniques. This shows significance in:
qa.e: They are the foundation for teaching and research in management.

qa.q: A principle that leads to specialisation helps firms adjust to new technology. Which significance is this?
qa.e: Flexible principles help organisations adapt to a dynamic environment.

qa.q: Fair remuneration and equity are principles that also help a firm to:
qa.e: Treating employees fairly is part of a business's responsibility to society.

qa.q: Principles of management improve managers' knowledge, ability and understanding of situations. This is called:
qa.e: Better understanding of real situations is the 'useful insights' significance.

qa.q: Which significance of principles helps managers avoid wastage and limit personal bias in running the organisation?
qa.a: Optimum utilisation of resources and effective administration
qa.e: Principles guide efficient use of resources and impartial administration.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Principles of management help in optimum utilisation of resources. Reason (R): They indicate cause-and-effect relationships, so managers can avoid wasteful trial and error.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Knowing likely effects helps managers choose actions that avoid waste, so R explains A.

qa.q: Without principles, managers would have to learn only by trial and error. This would most likely lead to:
qa.e: Trial and error is slow and costly; principles save this effort.

qa.q: Who is known as the father of scientific management?
qa.e: Frederick Winslow Taylor developed scientific management.

qa.q: 'Mental revolution' is associated with which principle of Taylor?
qa.e: Taylor said harmony needs a complete change of attitude, a mental revolution.

qa.q: Replacing guesswork and trial-and-error with scientific study of work is the principle of:
qa.e: Rule of thumb means guesswork; Taylor wanted science instead.

qa.q: Rangoli Garments selects workers through tests suited to each job and trains them to reach their best. Which principle is applied?
qa.a: Development of each and every person to his or her greatest efficiency and prosperity
qa.e: Scientific selection and training to reach full efficiency is this principle.

qa.q: Under 'cooperation, not individualism', management should:
qa.a: Reward suggestions from workers and involve them in decisions
qa.e: Taylor wanted close cooperation; management should value workers' suggestions.

qa.q: Taylor defined scientific management as knowing exactly what you want people to do and seeing that they do it in the:
qa.e: His definition stresses the best and cheapest way.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Taylor's 'harmony, not discord' requires a change in attitude of both management and workers. Reason (R): Taylor believed that the gains from scientific management should be shared between management and workers.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: When gains are shared, both sides stop seeing each other as rivals, which is the mental revolution needed for harmony.

qa.q: A supervisor decides a worker's daily target by guessing from past experience. Which principle of Taylor is violated?
qa.e: Guessing from experience is rule of thumb, which Taylor rejected.

qa.q: Functional foremanship is based on the separation of:
qa.e: Taylor separated planning and doing, with specialists for each.

qa.q: How many specialist foremen does a worker report to under functional foremanship?
qa.e: Four under the planning in-charge and four under the production in-charge make eight.

qa.q: Which foreman is responsible for keeping machines and tools ready for operation?
qa.e: The gang boss keeps machines and tools ready; the repair boss maintains their working condition.

qa.q: Which of these works under the planning in-charge?
qa.e: Planning in-charge: instruction card clerk, route clerk, time and cost clerk, disciplinarian.

qa.q: Functional foremanship violates which principle of Fayol?
qa.e: One worker gets orders from eight bosses, which goes against having one boss.

qa.q: Eliminating unnecessary varieties, sizes and dimensions of a product is called:
qa.e: Simplification removes needless diversity; standardisation sets benchmarks.

qa.q: Kiran Cement sets a fixed specification for raw material, mixing time and quality for every batch. This is:
qa.e: Setting standards for processes, materials and methods is standardisation.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Functional foremanship is an extension of the principle of division of work and specialisation. Reason (R): Under it, each foreman specialises in one aspect of the work.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Because each foreman handles one specialised function, it extends division of work to the shop floor.

qa.q: Which technique aims at eliminating unnecessary movements of workers?
qa.e: Motion study analyses movements like lifting and bending to remove wasteful ones.

qa.q: The standard time taken to perform a well-defined job is fixed by:
qa.e: Time study determines the standard time for a job.

qa.q: Deciding the amount and frequency of rest intervals is the purpose of:
qa.e: Fatigue study finds how often and how long workers should rest.

qa.q: Standard output is 20 units. Rates are ₹30 per unit at or above standard and ₹25 per unit below it. Ravi makes 22 units. What is his wage?
qa.e: Ravi reaches the standard, so the higher rate applies to all his units.

qa.q: Same scheme: standard 20 units; ₹30 at or above, ₹25 below. Sunil makes 18 units. What is his wage?
qa.e: Sunil is below standard, so the lower rate of ₹25 applies.

qa.q: Standard 10 units; ₹60 per unit at or above standard, ₹50 below. Worker P makes 10 units and worker Q makes 9. By how much does P earn more than Q?
qa.e: P earns 10 x 60 = ₹600; Q earns 9 x 50 = ₹450; the gap is ₹150, much more than one unit's worth.

qa.q: Finding the one best way of doing a job, covering everything from raw material to delivery, is:
qa.e: Method study looks at the whole way the job is done to find the best method.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The differential piece wage system motivates inefficient workers to improve. Reason (R): Under this system, workers who reach the standard are paid a higher rate per unit.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Because a small rise in output can move a worker to the higher rate and sharply raise wages, R explains A.

qa.q: Who is called the father of general management?
qa.e: Fayol gave the 14 general principles of management.

qa.q: An employee should receive orders from only one superior. This is the principle of:
qa.e: Unity of command means one boss for each employee.

qa.q: Sky Ltd makes shoes and bags, with a separate head and plan for each product division. This is:
qa.e: Each group of activities with the same objective has one head and one plan.

qa.q: A manager is made responsible for meeting a sales target but is given no authority to offer discounts. Which principle is violated?
qa.e: Responsibility without matching authority breaks the balance this principle requires.

qa.q: Fayol said discipline requires good superiors at all levels, clear and fair agreements and:
qa.e: Fayol wanted penalties applied fairly and with judgement.

qa.q: A manager pushes the company to buy from his relative's firm at a higher price. Which principle is violated?
qa.a: Subordination of individual interest to general interest
qa.e: Personal interest is placed above the organisation's interest.

qa.q: What is one consequence of violating unity of command?
qa.a: Confusion and a threat to discipline
qa.e: Dual subordination confuses employees and weakens authority and discipline.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Unity of command and unity of direction mean the same thing. Reason (R): Unity of command concerns a single employee, while unity of direction concerns the organisation as a whole.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true and gives the very difference between the two principles.

qa.q: Which principle says there should be a place for everything and everyone, and everything and everyone should be in its place?
qa.e: That is Fayol's statement of the principle of order.

qa.q: The 'gang plank' is linked with which principle?
qa.e: It is a shortcut in the scalar chain for emergencies.

qa.q: At Prime Logistics, women supervisors are denied promotions given to equally qualified men. Which principle is violated?
qa.e: Equity forbids discrimination on grounds such as sex.

qa.q: A manager says, 'We achieved this target,' instead of 'I achieved it.' This reflects:
qa.e: Fayol advised managers to replace 'I' with 'We' to build team spirit.

qa.q: A company invites employees to submit improvement ideas and implements the good ones. Which principle is followed?
qa.e: Encouraging employees to develop and carry out their own plans is initiative.

qa.q: When can the gang plank be used under the scalar chain?
qa.a: In an emergency, between employees at the same level
qa.e: Fayol allowed direct contact at the same level when quick communication is needed.

qa.q: A bank frequently transfers trained officers every few weeks. Which principle is violated?
qa.e: Employees need a reasonable tenure to perform well; frequent moves break stability.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Fayol suggested that every organisation should be fully decentralised. Reason (R): According to Fayol, there should be a balance between centralisation and decentralisation.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: Fayol never recommended full decentralisation; he asked for a balance. So A is false and R is true.

qa.q: Whose principles are based on observation and experimentation?
qa.e: Taylor developed his ideas through experiments; Fayol drew on personal experience.

qa.q: Which statement about unity of command is correct?
qa.a: Fayol strongly supported it, while Taylor did not consider it important
qa.e: Fayol made it a principle; Taylor's functional foremanship has eight bosses.

qa.q: Fayol's principles are mainly concerned with:
qa.e: Fayol focused on general administration; Taylor on productivity.

qa.q: A case says a firm pays a higher rate to workers meeting the standard and a lower rate to others. Which technique is this?
qa.e: Two rates linked to standard output is Taylor's differential piece wage system.

qa.q: In a company, the production manager and quality manager both instruct the same worker on the same task, and the worker is confused. Which principle of Fayol is violated?
qa.e: Getting orders from two superiors breaks unity of command.

qa.q: Ravi Electronics keeps a fixed place for every tool, and workers can find tools quickly. Which principle is applied?
qa.e: A place for everything, and everything in its place, is order.

qa.q: Taylor's perspective on management was from the:
qa.e: Taylor studied work on the shop floor; Fayol from the top.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Taylor did not consider unity of command important. Reason (R): Taylor's principles were formed through observation and experimentation.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true. The real reason for A is functional foremanship, under which a worker gets orders from eight specialist foremen; the basis of formation does not explain it.

qa.q: Business environment refers to:
qa.a: The total of individuals, institutions and forces outside the firm's control that may affect its performance
qa.e: It is external and beyond the firm's control.

qa.q: Customers, suppliers, competitors and investors are examples of:
qa.e: They directly affect the operations of a particular firm.

qa.q: A health-and-fitness trend raises demand for low-sugar drinks, which leads to new entrants and new labelling rules. Which feature is shown?
qa.e: One change triggers others; the forces are linked.

qa.q: The IT industry finds it very hard to predict which technology will dominate in five years. This reflects:
qa.e: Future environmental changes are hard to predict.

qa.q: Demand for woollen clothes is high in Himachal Pradesh but low in Kerala. Which feature is illustrated?
qa.e: The same environment affects firms differently in different regions.

qa.q: Economic, social, political, legal and technological conditions are called general forces because they:
qa.e: General forces affect all businesses, though indirectly.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Business environment is complex. Reason (R): It consists of many inter-related and dynamic forces that are difficult to understand in totality.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: R gives the reason for complexity: many linked, changing forces.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT a feature of business environment?
qa.a: It is fully controlled by the firm
qa.e: Business environment is, by definition, outside the firm's control.

qa.q: Being the first to spot an opportunity and use it before competitors is called:
qa.e: Moving first on an opportunity gives the firm a lead.

qa.q: A business gets finance, machines, raw material and workers from its environment. This importance is:
qa.e: The environment supplies the resources a firm needs.

qa.q: Learning about a new competitor's entry in advance helps a firm to:
qa.a: Identify threats and early warning signals
qa.e: Advance news of a threat lets the firm prepare.

qa.q: After the government announced new e-commerce rules, Bharat Mart revised its seller policy. Which importance is this?
qa.a: Assisting in planning and policy formulation
qa.e: Environmental changes guide a firm's plans and policies.

qa.q: Which statement about importance of business environment is correct?
qa.a: It helps firms cope with rapid changes
qa.e: Awareness of the environment helps firms respond to fast changes.

qa.q: Firms that keep monitoring the environment and adapt continuously tend to:
qa.e: Continuous monitoring improves performance.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Understanding business environment helps a firm to identify threats. Reason (R): A threat is any environmental development that may hinder the firm's performance.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Knowing what threats are, and watching for them, lets the firm spot them early. R explains A.

qa.q: Healthy Harvest saw a rising demand for organic food and launched an organic range before others. Which importance is shown?
qa.e: Spotting a positive trend early and acting first is identifying opportunities and getting first-mover advantage.

qa.q: A rise in interest rates by banks is part of which dimension?
qa.e: Interest rates are an economic factor.

qa.q: Rising demand for diet drinks due to health awareness belongs to the:
qa.e: Health and fitness trends are social trends.

qa.q: E-commerce platforms changing how people shop is an example of the:
qa.e: New methods of doing business through innovation are technological.

qa.q: Which of these is an element of the economic environment?
qa.e: Disposable income affects purchasing power, an economic factor.

qa.q: Gift-box sales of Mehta Sweets triple during the festive season every year. Which dimension explains this?
qa.e: Festivals and traditions are part of the social environment.

qa.q: Traditional watchmakers lost sales when digital watches arrived. This change came from the:
qa.e: A new technology replaced an older product.

qa.q: Inflation rises sharply. What is the most direct effect on a business?
qa.a: Costs of inputs rise and buyers' purchasing power may fall
qa.e: Inflation is an economic factor that raises prices of inputs and reduces real income.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The rising number of working women is a part of the social environment. Reason (R): Social environment includes social trends and changes in the lifestyle of people.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: More women working is a social trend and a change in lifestyle, so R explains why A is classified as social.

qa.q: A stable government and peaceful conditions attract investors. This relates to the:
qa.e: Political stability is a key political factor.

qa.q: A new law requiring nutrition labels on packaged foods is part of the:
qa.e: Legislation forms the legal environment.

qa.q: Which is a source of the legal environment?
qa.e: Laws, administrative orders and court judgements make up the legal environment.

qa.q: A ban on advertising of alcoholic drinks belongs to which dimension?
qa.e: It is a legal restriction on business.

qa.q: Classify: 'Banks cut lending rates, making car loans cheaper.'
qa.e: Interest rates are economic.

qa.q: Classify: 'More young people prefer to rent rather than buy furniture.'
qa.e: Changing preferences and lifestyle are social trends.

qa.q: Classify: 'A food startup uses AI to predict daily demand and reduce waste.'
qa.e: AI is a new method arising from innovation.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Political environment affects business. Reason (R): Political stability builds the confidence of business firms to invest.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Stability encourages investment, which is a key way politics affects business. R explains A.

qa.q: Demonetisation in India in 2016 withdrew the legal tender status of:
qa.e: Only the old ₹500 and ₹1000 notes ceased to be legal tender.

qa.q: In which year did the Government of India announce demonetisation of ₹500 and ₹1000 notes?
qa.e: It was announced on 8 November 2016.

qa.q: Requiring people to deposit old notes in banks, so unaccounted cash came under scrutiny, shows demonetisation as:
qa.e: It brought hidden cash into the tax system.

qa.q: Which was NOT an aim of demonetisation?
qa.a: Increasing the amount of cash in circulation permanently
qa.e: Demonetisation aimed at a less-cash economy, not more cash.

qa.q: After demonetisation, many people opened bank accounts and deposited their cash savings. This feature is:
qa.a: Channelising savings into the formal financial system
qa.e: Money moved from homes into banks, the formal system.

qa.q: A rise in use of mobile wallets and UPI after demonetisation reflects the aim of:
qa.e: Digital payments reduce reliance on cash.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Demonetisation helped in curbing counterfeit currency. Reason (R): Old ₹500 and ₹1000 notes, including fake ones, ceased to be legal tender.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Once the old notes lost legal tender status, fake notes of those denominations became useless. R explains A.

qa.q: For a business, demonetisation is best classified as a change in its:
qa.a: Economic environment brought about by a government policy decision
qa.e: It changed the money supply and payment conditions, an economic shift caused by government policy.

qa.q: Planning is best defined as:
qa.a: Deciding in advance what to do and how to do it
qa.e: That is the standard definition of planning.

qa.q: Why is planning called the primary function of management?
qa.a: Because it lays down the base for all other functions
qa.e: Organising, staffing, directing and controlling are done within the plans.

qa.q: Planning that involves forecasting future conditions shows that it is:
qa.e: Planning looks ahead into the future.

qa.q: If there were only one possible way to do a task, there would be no need for planning. This is because planning:
qa.e: Planning means choosing from alternatives; with one option there is nothing to decide.

qa.q: A one-year plan of Pallavi Crafts ends in March, and a new plan begins in April based on the old one's results. This shows planning is:
qa.e: Plans follow one after another without a break.

qa.q: Planning requires foresight, imagination and sound judgement. This shows planning is:
qa.e: It is an intellectual activity of thinking before doing.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Planning is pervasive. Reason (R): Planning is required at all levels of management and in all departments of the organisation.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: R gives the meaning of pervasiveness, so it explains A.

qa.q: Which feature of planning says that it is purposeful and has no meaning unless it contributes to predetermined goals?
qa.e: Plans are made to achieve objectives.

qa.q: Planning provides the standards against which actual performance is measured. This shows planning:
qa.e: Controlling compares actual results with standards set in plans.

qa.q: Which statement about planning and uncertainty is correct?
qa.a: Planning reduces the risks of uncertainty but cannot eliminate them
qa.e: Managers anticipate changes, but the future can never be fully predicted.

qa.q: A clear plan tells employees in advance what is to be done and how. This is:
qa.e: Knowing in advance what to do gives direction.

qa.q: Planning helps managers choose the best course from several alternatives. This importance is:
qa.e: Planning involves evaluating and selecting among alternatives.

qa.q: While planning a new snack line, Kesar Foods' managers came up with a millet-based idea. Which importance does this reflect?
qa.e: Planning encourages managers to think of new ideas.

qa.q: Planning coordinates activities of different departments so that work is not duplicated. This is:
qa.e: Planning removes duplication and waste.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Planning establishes standards for controlling. Reason (R): Planning provides the goals against which actual performance is compared.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Plans set goals; controlling measures performance against them. R explains A.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Planning eliminates the risk of uncertainty. Reason (R): Planning helps managers anticipate future changes and prepare for them.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false because planning only reduces risk. R is true.

qa.q: Managers continue with a plan even when circumstances have changed. Which limitation is this?
qa.e: Feeling bound to the original plan causes rigidity.

qa.q: Middle managers at Orbit Ltd are not allowed to deviate from plans framed by the top. Which limitation is highlighted?
qa.e: Following plans without freedom limits initiative and creativity.

qa.q: A company's sales plan failed because a new competitor entered with low prices. This shows planning:
qa.a: May not work in a dynamic environment
qa.e: Unexpected changes in the environment can make plans fail.

qa.q: 'Planning creates a false sense of security.' This relates to which limitation?
qa.e: Managers may rely on a past successful plan, but success needs proper implementation.

qa.q: Which is a limitation of planning?
qa.e: The others are importance points; time consumption is a limitation.

qa.q: Planning needs research, experts and many meetings. Which limitation follows?
qa.e: Time and money spent on planning can be large.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Planning may not work in a dynamic environment. Reason (R): The business environment is constantly changing and every change cannot be accurately foreseen.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Because changes cannot all be predicted, plans may fail. R explains A.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A well-made plan guarantees the success of a business. Reason (R): Success depends on proper implementation of the plan as well.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: plans need good execution. R is true.

qa.q: What is the first step in the planning process?
qa.e: Planning begins by deciding what is to be achieved.

qa.q: Assumptions about the future on which plans are based are called:
qa.e: Premises are the base assumptions of planning.

qa.q: Comparing the positive and negative aspects of each option in the light of objectives is:
qa.e: Evaluation weighs each option before the final choice.

qa.q: Tejas Motors decided to set up its new plant in Gujarat after comparing four states. Which step is this?
qa.e: The final choice is the selection step.

qa.q: Monitoring whether the plan is being carried out properly is called:
qa.e: Follow-up checks that the plan is being implemented as intended.

qa.q: Hiring staff and buying machines to put the chosen plan into action belongs to which step?
qa.e: Putting the plan into action is implementation, which may involve other functions such as organising and staffing.

qa.q: How many steps are there in the planning process as given in the NCERT book?
qa.e: Setting objectives, developing premises, identifying alternatives, evaluating alternatives, selecting an alternative, implementing, follow-up.

qa.q: Assertion (A): All managers in an organisation should be familiar with and use the same premises. Reason (R): Premises are the base on which plans are drawn, so using different assumptions would lead to inconsistent plans.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Since premises underlie plans, different premises would make departmental plans clash. R explains A.

qa.q: Which of these is a standing plan?
qa.e: Policies are used repeatedly; budgets, programmes and projects are single-use.

qa.q: A plan for organising a one-time product launch event is a:
qa.e: It is developed for a one-time event.

qa.q: 'To increase sales by 15% in the next financial year' is an example of a(n):
qa.e: It states a measurable end result with a time limit.

qa.q: A comprehensive plan that considers the business environment and decides long-term goals, course of action and allocation of resources is a:
qa.e: These three dimensions define a strategy.

qa.q: 'It is our company's practice to buy raw materials only from local suppliers wherever possible.' This is a:
qa.e: A general statement guiding decisions with some discretion ('wherever possible') is a policy.

qa.q: Which statement about policies is correct?
qa.a: They are general guidelines that leave room for discretion
qa.e: Policies guide thinking; rules allow no discretion; procedures list steps; budgets use numbers.

qa.q: Which is NOT a dimension of strategy?
qa.a: Listing the steps for issuing a gate pass
qa.e: Step-by-step lists are procedures, not strategy.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Budgets are single-use plans. Reason (R): A budget is prepared for a specific period and a new one is made for the next period.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Because each budget applies to one period and is replaced, it is single-use. R explains A.

qa.q: A plan that tells the exact sequence of steps to perform an activity is a:
qa.e: Procedures list chronological steps.

qa.q: 'Employees must not use the company printer for personal work.' This is a:
qa.e: It is a specific must-not with no discretion.
